exp.4:3:
Paul says that while we live in this body, which he calls a "tabernacle" (a tent, something temporary), we feel the weight and we groan. We do not want to be found "naked," that is, without a body, but to be "clothed upon," that is, to receive a new body over the present one. In this way, what is mortal would be "swallowed up," taken in by eternal life.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth and speaks of his own sufferings and weaknesses. He compares the present body to a fragile tent and the future body to a heavenly dwelling. God himself prepared us for this and gave us the Spirit as a guarantee. Christians interpret in different ways what happens just after death, but the final hope is clear.

For today: when tiredness, sickness or pain weigh on you, do not lose heart. Your hope is not merely to endure, but the full life God has promised. Ask the Spirit to remind you of that promise every day.
exp.9:3:
It says that Paul and his companions are fighting a battle, but not with human methods or the methods of this world. The word "warfare" here means the struggle or service of a soldier, and the weapons are not "carnal," meaning they do not belong to human nature or work without God's help. Their weapons have power that comes from God and can pull down strongholds, that is, deeply rooted ideas and attitudes that resist the truth.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because some were accusing him of acting out of human interests. He admits that he lives in a weak body, but makes clear that his ministry does not depend on tricks or on his own strength. The verses that follow speak of pulling down arguments and bringing every thought into obedience to Christ.

For today: when you face a conflict or a lie that seems impossible to overcome, do not respond with pride or anger. Pray, use the truth of the Bible, and act with love and patience, trusting that God is at work.
exp.3:17:
The text says that Christians do not focus their attention on what can be seen with the eyes, but on what is not seen. The reason is simple: what is visible lasts only a short time ("temporal"), but what is invisible lasts forever ("eternal").

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Corinth. He tells them that he suffers persecution and exhaustion, but he does not give up. His body wears down, while his inner life is renewed each day. For this reason he looks beyond his present pain, toward the glory that God promises. Many understand that what is invisible includes God's promises and life with Him.

For today: when you are going through a trial, do not stay only looking at the problem. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible, remembering that God is still at work and that your hope does not depend on what you see.
exp.12:7:
It says that Paul and his companions have no power to oppose the truth; they can only act in its favor. The phrase "we can do nothing against" means "we can do nothing." The sentence shows that their authority is subject to what is true and is not used to twist it.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he has had tensions. Some doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. Before visiting them again, he tells them that he is not looking to look good or to win an argument. He would rather they do what is right, even if he is seen as having failed the test.

For today: when you correct or lead others, seek to serve the truth and not your pride. Ask yourself whether what you say or do helps build up the person, even if it does not make you look good.
exp.1:4:
If someone caused sorrow, he did not grieve me alone, but in part, and, to avoid overstating it, he grieved all of you. The word that the source uses for "caused grief" means made someone sad or caused pain. The phrase about not burdening you means that Paul did not want to press too hard or make the matter sound worse than it was.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. Someone in the community had committed a serious offense, and the whole church suffered for it. Paul avoids presenting himself as the only one wounded, and he does not want to load anyone with blame. Scholars debate who that person was and what the exact offense was, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when someone hurts us within the church or the family, let us remember that the pain is rarely ours alone. Let us speak with moderation, without exaggerating the offense, and seek correction that leads to forgiveness and restoration.
exp.3:3:
There is a spiritual power, called "the god of this world," that has blinded the minds of those who do not believe. The phrase "of this world" means of this present age or this present world. Because of that blindness, they cannot see the light of the gospel, which shows the glory of Christ, who is the exact image of God. Many understand that this "god" is Satan, although he is not a true God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry. He preaches with honesty, without deception. If someone does not understand the message, it is not because it is poorly explained, but because there is a spiritual blindness. Then he makes clear that he does not preach himself, but Jesus Christ as Lord.

Today we can pray for those who do not believe, instead of arguing with them or judging them. We present Christ with sincerity and trust that only God opens the eyes of the heart.
exp.4:11:
Paul says that he is not trying to commend himself to them again as someone trustworthy. Rather, he wants to give them reasons to be proud of him, so that they can answer those who boast in outward things and not in what is within. Commending oneself means recommending oneself, and boasting means taking pride in something.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some teachers criticized him and questioned his authority, relying on his appearance, their letters of recommendation, and their eloquence. Paul has just spoken of the judgment seat of Christ and of God knowing his heart. For that reason he does not defend himself out of pride, but so that the church will not be deceived. Some interpret that there is a touch of irony; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Today we can learn not to judge or admire people only by their outward image or visible success. Let us ask God to teach us to look at the heart, beginning with our own.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that God is the one who keeps us firm together with you in Christ, and that he is also the one who anointed us. "Stablisheth" means to establish, to make firm and secure. "Anointed" means to set someone apart for God and give them a task, as oil was used for this purpose in biblical times. The word "ye" is the "you" of today.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth. Some doubted him because he had changed his travel plans, and they saw him as someone who said "yes" and "no" at the same time. Paul answers that his message is trustworthy because it comes from God, who fulfills what he promises in Christ. His steadfastness does not depend on himself, but on God.

For today: when you feel unsure of your faith or your calling, remember that God is the one who sustains you. Rest in his faithfulness, and ask him to make you firm and trustworthy in what you say and do.
exp.10:20:
Paul says that he is ashamed to admit that, compared with the false apostles, he seemed "weak," that is, lacking strength, because he had not treated the Corinthians harshly. "Reproach" means shame or dishonor. He then adds that if others dare to boast about anything, he also dares to do so, though he acknowledges that speaking this way is "foolishness."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some arrogant teachers were dominating and exploiting the believers, and they were putting up with it. Paul does not want to boast, but he feels compelled to do so, with irony, to defend his ministry and to protect the believers from these deceptions.

Today we can learn not to be impressed by someone who speaks with great confidence or abuses their authority. Let us measure everything by the humble character of Christ, and value sincere service more than the appearance of power.
exp.11:15:
Paul says that he admits he was not a financial burden to the Corinthians. Then he repeats, with irony, what some were saying: that, being crafty, he had caught them by deceit. The quoted words in the source belong to the old wording, so I will give the sense in plain terms. "Burdened" means weighed down or loaded. "Crafty" here is an accusation, not a compliment. The phrase about catching them by deceit means that he would have trapped them with a trick.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against critics who doubted his honesty. Although he did not charge them, someone was suggesting that he had a hidden plan to profit from them. That is why, in the verses that follow, he mentions Titus and the brothers sent with him, and asks whether any of them took advantage of the church. His open life was his answer.

When someone serves with generosity, others sometimes doubt his motives. We can respond without anger, with openness and a good witness. And if we serve, let us examine our hearts to seek people, not their benefits.
exp.6:1:
Paul asks the Corinthians: "Receive us," that is, "make room for us in your hearts" or "receive us with confidence." Then he gives three reasons: we have wronged no one (harmed or treated anyone unjustly), we have corrupted no one (ruined them or led them astray), and we have defrauded no one (cheated or taken advantage of anyone).

Paul writes to a church with which he had experienced tensions. Some doubted his integrity. That is why, after inviting them to live in holiness, he asks them not to withhold their affection from him. In the following verse he clarifies that he is not condemning them, but loves them deeply. His conscience is at peace.

For today: when a relationship grows cold because of misunderstandings, let us seek reconciliation with humility and openness. Living with integrity allows us to ask for trust without fear, and it also reminds us to open our hearts to those who love us and correct us sincerely.
exp.4:1:
Because we live in a fragile body, believers sigh with longing. "Groan" means to sigh with both pain and hope. To be "clothed upon" means to be covered with something new, like putting a garment on over what you already wear. The "heavenly dwelling" is the new, eternal body that God promises, compared to a house.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which was going through trials, and he himself was suffering. He compares the present body to a tent, something temporary. Some understand that he is speaking of the resurrection; others think of an intermediate state after death. What is clear is that he wants to encourage them with hope.

For today: when weariness, sickness or pain weigh on you, do not hide your sigh. Bring it before God and remember that his promise is new life, not loss.
exp.6:11:
Paul says that when he wrote his earlier letter to the Corinthians, his main purpose was not to point out the one who committed the offense or to defend the one who suffered it. He wanted them to see clearly how much he cared for them, and to see it before God, that is, in complete sincerity. Care means genuine concern and interest.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth after a strained relationship. He had written them a strong letter, which caused them sorrow, and Titus brought him good news that they had responded with repentance. It is not known with certainty who the offender was; scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: when you have to correct someone, examine your motive. Let it not be to win an argument or to punish, but to show genuine care for that person, as God would.
exp.3:1:
Paul says that he and his companions have turned away from hidden and shameful things. He speaks of secret places to hide in, and of cunning or trickery. They do not manipulate or distort the message of God; instead they set out the truth plainly, so that every honest and sincere person can weigh it in the sight of God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom some doubted his integrity and his ministry. He maintains that his service is the fruit of God's mercy, and so he does not lose heart. His way of preaching is open and without tricks, and this prepares what follows about those who cannot see the gospel.

For today: teach and live your faith with transparency. Do not adjust or dress up God's message to please people or to gain advantage; let your conduct be seen without fear.
exp.7:0:
Paul tells the believers in Corinth about something God did in the churches of Macedonia. The words "we do you to wit" simply mean "we want you to know." The "grace of God" here is his favor and his generous work, which could be seen in the lives of those churches. "Bestowed on" is simply "given to."

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth, encouraging them to take part in a collection to help other Christians in need. To motivate them, he holds up as an example the churches of Macedonia, who were poor and suffering, yet still gave with joy, as the following verses show.

For today: generosity is a gift from God, not only our own effort. We can ask him to give us a willing heart, and to give joyfully according to what we have, without waiting to become rich before helping someone.
exp.2:11:
Paul says that because we have such a great hope, we speak with great confidence and openness. "Such hope" refers to the glory of the new covenant, which remains. "Great confidence" means speaking with clarity and boldness, without hiding anything.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defending his ministry. He compares the old covenant, given through Moses, with the new covenant in Christ and the Spirit. The old had glory, but it was temporary. The new is more glorious and remains. For this reason Paul preaches openly, without a veil, unlike Moses, who covered his face.

For today: if your hope is firmly in Christ, you do not need to speak of your faith with fear or in secret. You can share it with simplicity, honesty and courage, trusting that God works in hearts.
exp.5:13:
It says that believers should not join in a close and unequal relationship with the unbelievers, that is, with those who do not believe in Christ. The "yoke" was the wooden piece that joined two animals so they could plow together. Paul asks, using images of contrast, what righteousness and unrighteousness have in common, or what light has to do with darkness.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, whom he loves as his children. He asks them to open their hearts, and then he warns them against partnerships that would pull them away from God, since they are the temple of the living God. Interpreters debate whether he has in mind marriage, business, or idolatry; he probably includes several areas.

Today, before you commit to a partnership, a relationship, or an important project, ask yourself whether that union will bring you closer to God or pull you away from him. That does not prevent you from loving and treating everyone well.
exp.4:8:
It says that, because of what comes before, Paul and his companions strive to please God. The word "labour" means they put real effort and energy into something. The word "or" in the verse is the same as the "or" we use today, so the phrase means "whether absent or present." That is, whether they are still in this body or already with the Lord, their goal is the same: to be pleasing to him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about the hope of being with the Lord after death. Even so, he does not let that hope make him passive. Next he mentions that all of us will appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Some understand this as an evaluation of the Christian life, not as a condemnation. Paul also defends the sincerity of his ministry.

For today: make pleasing God your daily aim, not only at church but at work, at home, and in small decisions, trusting in his grace and not acting out of fear.
exp.11:13:
He says Paul is ready to visit the Corinthians for the third time. He assures them that he will not be a financial burden, because he does not seek their possessions but them. He uses a comparison: children do not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. The verse of the quoted words is left out here, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Paul speaks as an apostle and as the founder of that church. Some in Corinth questioned his authority, and he defends himself with irony, since he had not charged them anything. He presents himself as a spiritual father who gives without expecting payment, and his priority is their well-being.

For today: whoever serves others, in the church or in the family, should ask what they are seeking: what they can receive or the good of the people. True love gives first, without turning others into a source of profit.
exp.4:15:
It says that Paul and his companions no longer judge anyone by appearances, that is, by merely human standards: background, status, or outward look. The phrase "according to the flesh" means judging by the world's criteria. It adds that even Christ they once regarded in that way, but no longer. "We know" here refers to valuing or understanding someone, not just dealing with them.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had tensions, since some boasted about outward things and criticized him. Earlier he explained that the love of Christ drives him, because Christ died for all. For that reason he changed the way he looked at people. Scholars debate whether he once thought of Jesus only as a human teacher or as a rival, but the point is that now he sees him as Lord and Savior.

Today, before judging someone by their appearance, their money, or their past, ask yourself: "How does Christ see this person, the one for whom he died?" Ask God for a more loving way of seeing.
exp.1:16:
Paul says that he and his companions are not like the many who corrupt the word of God. Those who corrupt it are false traders, people who sell it or water it down to make a profit. The image may suggest a merchant who mixes or dilutes his goods. By contrast, they speak with sincerity, as those sent by God, aware that he sees them, and in union with Christ.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, and he has just spoken of the great responsibility of proclaiming the gospel, asking who is sufficient for such a task. He answers that it does not depend on their own strength or on personal gain. He is probably defending himself against criticism and against other teachers who sought benefit. Scholars debate exactly who they were, but the contrast with his own ministry is clear.

For today: before you teach or share the Bible, ask yourself what your motive is. Speak with honesty, without twisting the message to please people or to gain something, remembering that God is listening.
exp.5:10:
He says that Paul speaks to the Corinthians with complete frankness and holds nothing back. Speaking freely and honestly is what it means to speak openly. Their heart being enlarged means that his affection is wide, with plenty of room for them.

Paul writes to a church with which he had had tensions. He has just described the sufferings of his ministry, and now he shows them his affection. In the verses that follow, he tells them that the problem is not a lack of love on his part, but that they are closed off. He asks them to respond by opening their hearts to him too, as children would.

For today: if there is a cold or strained relationship, take the first step with sincerity and warmth. Speak with clarity, without bitterness, and leave room in your heart to be reconciled.
exp.5:15:
Paul asks what agreement there can be between the temple of God and idols. The answer is: none. He affirms that believers are the temple of the living God, citing Old Testament promises where God says he will live among his people and be their God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, a church surrounded by temples and idolatry. He asks them not to join together in a "yoke" (a bond that forces people to walk together) with those who do not believe. Scholars discuss whether he is speaking of marriage, business, or taking part in pagan worship; the text shows the general idea of not sharing loyalties.

For today: if God lives in you, be careful about what enters your life. Examine which friendships, commitments, or habits compete with your faith, and ask God for wisdom to live faithfully without despising anyone.
exp.11:1:
Paul speaks of a man "in Christ", that is, a believer, who fourteen years earlier was "caught up", carried away suddenly and forcefully, to the "third heaven". He does not know whether it happened in his body or out of his body; only God knows.

The one speaking is Paul, and almost everyone understands that he is talking about himself, although he tells it as if it were another person. He feels compelled to defend himself before some in Corinth who boasted of their spiritual experiences. About the "third heaven", it is thought to be the presence of God, but the text gives no further detail.

Today we can learn from Paul's humility. He kept this experience for fourteen years and did not use it to boast. If God gives us something valuable, it is not to show ourselves off, but to serve with simplicity and give glory to Christ.
exp.3:10:
Paul says that we who live as followers of Christ are always exposed to death for Jesus' sake. This is no accident: the purpose is that the life of Jesus may be seen in our weak and mortal body. "Always delivered unto death" means being in constant danger; "mortal flesh" refers to our fragile body.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, defending his ministry. He has suffered persecution, beatings and dangers for preaching the gospel. He explains that, although he seems weak, the power of God is shown precisely in that weakness. In this way, his suffering serves so that others may receive life.

For today: when you go through trials or exhaustion from following Jesus, do not think that God has forgotten you. Ask him that, in the midst of your weariness, others may see his patience, his love and his hope in you.
exp.6:15:
Paul says that he rejoices because he can have full confidence in the Corinthians. The word "rejoice" means joy, and "confidence" means that he feels assurance and hope in them. The word "you" refers to the Corinthian believers themselves.

Paul writes this letter to a church with which he had tensions. He had sent them a strong letter of correction, and Titus brought him good news: they received it well and showed obedience. Paul had already spoken well of them to Titus, and this proved true. For that reason he ends this topic with relief and joy. It is an expression of reconciliation.

Today we can learn to encourage others with sincere words of trust. If someone has corrected their course or has improved a relationship, let us acknowledge that change with gratitude, instead of continuing to remember only the past. Expressed trust can strengthen the one who receives it.
exp.4:20:
Jesus, who never sinned, was treated as a sinner in our place, so that we might be declared righteous before God through him. The phrase "made sin" is usually understood to mean that he bore our guilt or was offered as a sacrifice for sin; interpreters explain it in several different ways. Being "the righteousness of God" speaks of being right with God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. He has just said that God, through Christ, reconciles the world to himself and that believers are his ambassadors. This verse explains the reason for the appeal: "Be reconciled to God." Reconciliation is possible because of what Christ did.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor by your own efforts. When you feel unworthy, remember that your standing before God rests in Christ. Come to him with confidence, and share that same message of peace with others.
exp.7:19:
This verse says that Paul and his team want to prevent anyone from criticizing them or speaking badly of them for the way they handle this large gift. The word "blame" in the verse above is the word the verse is describing: it means to criticize, find fault with, or accuse harshly. "This abundance which is administered by us" refers to the large amount of money they are managing and carrying.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish their gift for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. Since it involves a great deal of money, he takes care that everything is done in an orderly way and that others accompany and oversee the handling of it. In this way no one can suspect him.

For today: if you handle money belonging to the church or to other people, do everything with transparency and as a team. Being accountable is not distrust; it is a way of protecting the witness and the trust of everyone.
exp.7:9:
Paul says he is going to give his opinion, not a command, about the offering for the poor believers. It is good for the Corinthians to finish what they started. They were the first, since last year, not only to make the offering but even to want to give it. "It is good for you" means it does them good, and "to want to do it" refers to having the desire to give.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. They had promised to help the struggling believers in Jerusalem, but the project had lost its momentum. Paul does not press them with authority. He reminds them of the example of Christ, who became poor out of love for them, and he invites them to respond with sincerity.

For today: think of something good you promised or wanted to do, such as helping someone or supporting a need, that was left half finished. Take one concrete step today to complete it, with joy and according to what you have.
exp.3:9:
Paul says that he and his companions always carry, in their own bodies, the "death of Jesus," that is, sufferings similar to those he himself endured. But this has a purpose: that the life of Jesus, his power and his strength, may also be seen in those same weak bodies. "Made manifest" means shown, made visible.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and speaks of the hardships he suffers while preaching the gospel. The verses before this one show the contrast: they strike him, but they do not destroy him. He says that we are like clay jars, fragile, so that the power may be seen as coming from God and not from us. Some understand the "death" as real persecution; others understand it as a life of daily self-giving.

For today: when you are tired, limited, or going through a trial, do not hide it or become discouraged. Ask God that, in the midst of your weakness, others may see his strength and his hope in you.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that the believers in Jerusalem, when they receive the help, will pray for the Corinthians and feel affection for them. They will do so as they see the surpassing grace, that is, the extraordinary kindness God gave them to be generous. The phrase "long after you" means they deeply desire and yearn for you, and "for the exceeding grace of God in you" refers to the grace God has given you.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to encourage them to complete the offering for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He explains that their help not only meets needs, but also produces thanksgiving to God and unites believers from different peoples, Jews and non-Jews. Some scholars also see here a sign of unity between both groups, although the text does not say it in those words.

For today: when you give or serve others, do it with humility, knowing that generosity comes from God. And when someone helps you, pray for that person. In this way the bonds of love in the church are strengthened.
exp.5:1:
He says that God heard and helped his people at a favorable time. "Acceptable time" means a time when God receives people and shows his favor. "Day of salvation" is a day of salvation or rescue. "Helped" means assisted. Paul affirms that this moment is now.

Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8, where God speaks to his Servant. He writes to the Corinthians and urges them, together with his co-workers, not to receive God's grace in vain, that is, without it producing fruit in their lives. This letter follows a period of tension between Paul and that church, and that is why he insists that they respond to God. Some understand "now" as the age of the gospel; others, as an urgent invitation to that congregation.

Today it is not wise to put off what God is asking of you. If you sense his call to forgive, to return to him, or to change something, respond today with humility and trust in his grace.
exp.9:15:
Paul says that his desire is to carry the gospel to places farther than Corinth, where no one has yet preached it. He does not want to step into the field of work that belongs to others and boast about what was already "made ready" by someone else.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, and some teachers were criticizing him and taking credit for work that was not theirs. Paul answers that he stays within the field God gave him. He hopes that their faith will grow so that his work can reach further, and he ends by saying that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.

Today we can serve with humility, do well what God has entrusted to us, and rejoice in what others do, without competing or claiming the credit for what they have built.
exp.12:10:
Paul closes his letter with some final words to the brothers and sisters. He asks them to rejoice, to strive to grow toward maturity, to allow themselves to be comforted, to think in harmony, and to live in peace. He promises that the God of peace and of love will be with them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he has had tensions over divisions and failures in conduct. He writes from a distance so that he will not have to be harsh when he arrives, since his authority is for building up and not for tearing down. His farewell is warm and pastoral.

For today: if there are disagreements in your family or in your church, seek peace and humility first, rather than winning the argument. God accompanies those who work to live in harmony.
exp.10:18:
Paul says with irony that the Corinthians, who think they are wise, gladly put up with fools. The word "suffer" means to endure or put up with, and "gladly" means with pleasure. It is a gentle but firm rebuke.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which he founded. Some "super-apostles" came boasting of their achievements and questioning Paul. He feels compelled to boast as well, though he calls it "foolishness," to show how absurd that kind of pride is. The verses that follow explain that the Corinthians were enduring abuse from these leaders.

For today: do not admire someone simply because they speak with confidence or boast of success. Examine with humility, in the light of the Bible, what they teach and how they treat people, and do not tolerate abuse in the name of spiritual authority.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that whoever is united to Christ is a "new creature," that is, a new creation. The "old things" (the way of living without God, centered on oneself) have passed away, and something new has begun. The phrase "behold" can be read as "look" or "notice."

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Corinth. He had just explained that Christ died and rose again for everyone, so that we would no longer live for ourselves. For this reason he says that we no longer judge anyone by outward appearances. He then adds that this change comes from God, who reconciled us to himself.

For today: if you are in Christ, your past does not define who you are. You can ask God for help in leaving behind an old habit and living this week with a more generous and reconciling heart.
exp.4:4:
He tells us that God himself has prepared us for a new and eternal life, what Paul calls being "clothed upon," with a glorious body. As a guarantee of that promise, God has given us his Spirit. The word "earnest" means a first payment or deposit: something that assures us the rest will come.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He is speaking about the frailty of the body we have now, which he describes as a temporary tent. He groans and suffers, but he does not lose hope. His confidence is not in himself, but in what God has already begun to do.

For today: when you feel tired or limited, remember that the Holy Spirit within you is God's promise that what is best is still to come. Rest in his faithfulness and not only in what you can see.
exp.1:9:
When the church forgives someone, Paul also forgives him. And if he has forgiven anything, he did it for their sake, "in the person of Christ," that is, in the presence of Christ or as his representative. The phrase "if I forgave any thing" shows humility: Paul does not insist on personal offenses.

Paul writes to the Corinthians after a painful situation in which someone had caused trouble and the church had disciplined him. Now that this person seems repentant, Paul asks them to restore him with love and joins in their forgiveness. He does this so that they will not gain sorrow or Satan's deception, as the following verse says. Scholars debate who exactly that person was.

For today: when someone truly repents, let us not keep the punishment longer than necessary. Let us forgive with humility, knowing that Christ forgave us, and help restore the relationship.
exp.7:13:
It says that the Corinthians, who at that moment had more, should help the believers in need in Jerusalem. In this way, if someday the Corinthians find themselves in need, those others could help them in return. "Abundance" is what is left over; "want" is what is lacking; "supply" is to complete or cover what is lacking; "equality" is a fair sharing, where no one is left without what is necessary.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He is encouraging them to finish the offering they had promised for the poor brothers and sisters in Judea. He makes clear that he does not want them to be squeezed while others rest. He asks for generosity according to what they have, given with a willing heart. Some understand that Paul is speaking only of material help; the text shows it this way in this passage.

Today, if you have more than you need, think of someone close to you who is in need and help them with joy. Remember that all of us may need help someday.
exp.10:2:
Paul says he is afraid that the Corinthians may be deceived, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness. He fears that their minds may be corrupted and drawn away from the sincerity that is in Christ: a wholehearted devotion, without mixture or entanglement.

Paul is writing to the believers in Corinth, whom he himself brought to the gospel. He describes himself as a father who betrothed them to Christ as a pure bride. He is concerned that some teachers who came later may present them with a different Jesus and a different gospel, and that they may accept them far too easily.

Today, when we hear new or very striking teachings, it is wise to compare them with what Jesus has already shown us in the Bible. If an idea complicates the faith or changes who Christ is, it should be examined calmly and in prayer before it is accepted.
exp.2:13:
It says that the minds of many Israelites became hardened or dull. "Were dulled" means they lost their edge, without being able to understand well. Even today, when the Old Testament is read, it is as if a veil covered its meaning. Paul affirms that this veil is taken away only through Christ. "But" is the same as "but."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and compares his ministry with that of Moses, who covered his face when he came down from the mountain. Paul speaks of his own countrymen, who read the law without recognizing Christ in it. Some understand the end that was to be abolished as the close of the old covenant, and others interpret it in other ways.

For today: when you read the Bible, ask God to open your understanding and look for Christ on every page. He gives light to those who come near with humility.
exp.9:1:
Paul asks the Corinthians that, when he comes to visit them, he will not have to be harsh or bold. He says he is determined to act with firmness toward certain people who think he lives according to the flesh, that is, guided by weak or self-interested human motives.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. Some critics said he was brave in his letters but weak and insignificant in person. He answers that his gentleness imitates Christ and is not weakness. He prefers to correct them now with love so that he will not have to do it with severity later.

For today: if you have authority, in the family, the church, or at work, try to correct first with patience and humility. And if you are criticized unjustly, do not respond with pride; respond with truth and gentleness, as Christ did.
exp.12:9:
That is why Paul writes this letter from a distance: he wants the Corinthians to correct themselves before he arrives, so that he will not have to be harsh with them when he is with them. The "authority" is the authority the Lord gave him, and "harshness" is a severe way of dealing with people. That authority is for building up, that is, for constructing and strengthening faith, and not for tearing down.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth, with which he had had tensions, since some questioned his authority. In this farewell he asks them to change and to seek maturity, and he reminds them that his aim is not to impose himself but to help them grow in the truth.

For today: if you have some authority, in the home, the church, or the workplace, use it to lift people up and not to humiliate them. And if someone corrects you with love, use that time to set straight whatever needs fixing.
exp.9:11:
Paul says that he does not dare to put himself in the same group or to compare himself with certain men who commend themselves. Those people use their own yardstick to measure themselves: they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves among themselves. Paul concludes that this is not having understanding; in other words, they are not wise.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had tension. Some were criticizing him, saying that his letters were strong but that in person he was weak and spoke without impact. In response, he uses irony about those who recommend themselves, and he explains that his authority comes from the task God gave him, not from his own opinion.

For today: do not use your own standard or comparison with others as the measure of your worth or your service. Ask yourself what God has entrusted to you, and be faithful in that, with humility.
exp.0:14:
Paul says that, trusting that the Corinthians understood his heart and knew that he was sincere, he wanted to visit them first. His desire was that they would receive a second benefit, that is, a second blessing or kindness. Some versions say "double joy" or "double favor." The word "minded" means "had the intention of."

Paul writes to a church with which he had tensions. Some criticized him because he had changed his travel plans and said that he could not be trusted. Here he begins to explain that his plans came from affection for them, not from whim or deceit. The exact details of that visit are not fully known.

For today: when you have to change a commitment, explain your reasons with humility and honesty. Seek to bless others, and do not let a misunderstanding cool your relationships.
exp.5:9:
Paul and his companions go through sorrow, yet they have a joy that does not go out. They are poor, yet through their service they make many rich spiritually. They have nothing in a material sense, yet they possess everything in Christ. The word "sorrowful" means full of grief; the phrase about making many rich is understood as giving spiritual riches to others.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. Some doubted him. That is why he describes his ministry through contrasts: he suffers, but he does not lose hope. Right after this, he opens his heart to them and asks them to answer him with the same closeness.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can weep and, at the same time, rest in Christ. That joy does not depend on circumstances, but on what you already have in God. Ask him to renew it in you today.
exp.3:8:
He says that although Paul and his companions suffer persecution, God does not leave them alone. To be "forsaken" means to be left behind, abandoned. To be "cast down" means to be knocked over, thrown to the ground, and yet they are not destroyed. To "perish" means to die or come to an end.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth and defends his ministry. He says that he carries the treasure of the gospel in fragile jars of clay, that is, in frail bodies. In this way it is clear that the strength comes from God and not from them. His sufferings unite him to Jesus, so that the life of Christ may be seen in him.

When you go through rejection, exhaustion, or hard blows, do not confuse weakness with abandonment. You can fall without being destroyed. Tell God honestly what you feel and rest in the knowledge that his power sustains you, even in your most fragile days.
exp.4:10:
Paul says that the fear of the Lord controls him, and for that reason he tries to persuade people. Here "fear" means a deep, reverent respect toward God, not a fear that paralyzes. Being moved by that respect is what drives him. God sees his heart clearly, and Paul hopes that the consciences of the Corinthians will also recognize him as sincere.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had doubted his honesty and his ministry. He has just reminded them that everyone will appear before the judgment seat of Christ. For that reason he insists that his way of serving is open and that his motivation is to please God, not to impress people.

For today: live out and share your faith knowing that God knows your motives. Before you speak or serve, ask yourself: "Am I doing this to please God and truly help, or to look good?" Ask him to keep your heart sincere.
exp.4:13:
It says that the love of Christ moves us, presses us, and guides us, like a force that will not let a person stay still. "Constrains" is an old word that means to press tightly or to control. Paul reaches this conclusion: if Christ died for all, then all died with him. This last point is understood in several ways: that all of us were lost and needed his death, or that whoever trusts in Christ dies with him to their old life.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the Corinthians. He is defending his ministry against those who boasted in outward things. He explains that his devotion, which some considered madness, springs from the love of Christ and not from self-interest.

For today: before serving or correcting others, ask yourself what moves you. If the love of Christ motivates you, you will serve with more patience, humility, and steadiness, without seeking applause.
exp.6:10:
Paul reminds the Corinthians what the godly sorrow produced in them: earnestness (care), a desire to clear themselves (defense), indignation against wrong (anger), reverence for God (fear), a longing to restore the relationship (strong desire), enthusiasm for doing what is right (zeal), and a willingness to correct the wrong (vindication, that is, to set things right). At the end he says that in this matter they proved themselves to be clear, meaning free of blame for continuing to tolerate the wrong.

Paul had written them a strong letter about a sin the church had tolerated. Titus brought the news that they had repented, and Paul rejoices, not because they were sad, but because of the change that followed.

For today: when someone corrects us, let us not run away or defend ourselves with pride. Let us ask whether this is a sorrow that draws us closer to God and moves us to truly change.
exp.10:26:
Paul lists more of the hardships he endured while serving Christ: hard work and exhaustion, sleepless nights, hunger and thirst, frequent fasting, and cold and not having enough clothing. "Watchings," the sleepless nights, is the word used here for going without sleep. "Nakedness" here refers to not having adequate clothing, not to being without clothes at all. The "fastings" may have been voluntary or may have come from having no food; the text does not specify.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom some "super-apostles" boasted of their worth. Paul, with irony and sorrow, does not boast of successes but of his weaknesses, to show that his service was genuine and costly.

Today, this reminds us that serving God does not always look brilliant or comfortable. If you are tired or lacking necessities because you are doing good, you are not alone. Seek to value faithfulness above appearance, and pray for those who serve quietly.
exp.0:23:
Paul says that he and his companions do not want to lord it over the faith of the Corinthians, as if they were its owners. "Lording it over" means dominating or controlling. Rather, they see themselves as fellow workers who contribute to the Corinthians' joy. He also reminds them that they stand firm because of their own faith in Christ.

Paul is writing to a church with which he has had tensions. He has just explained that he did not go to Corinth so as not to cause them more sorrow or to have to correct them harshly. He wants to make clear that his authority as an apostle is not for pressuring, but for serving.

Today, those who teach or lead in the church, as well as parents or friends, can ask themselves: "Am I controlling, or am I helping others grow in their joy and in their faith?" Walking alongside others with respect, without manipulating them, strengthens people's trust in God.
exp.11:14:
He says Paul is willing, very gladly, to spend everything he has and even to be spent himself for the good of the Corinthians. The phrase "spend and be spent" means giving what one has and being used up completely for them. He also sadly acknowledges that the more he loves them, the less they love him.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he has a strained relationship. Some were criticizing him and doubting his authority. He did not charge them for preaching, and with irony he asks them to forgive him for that. He compares himself to a father who gives to his children, not to someone who seeks to get something from them.

For today: real love means giving without conditions, even when we do not receive the same affection in return. We can keep serving someone with patience, without charging them or expecting gratitude, trusting that God sees that love.
exp.1:7:
It says that Paul asks the Corinthians to show their love toward a person again. Here, to show love means to reaffirm it clearly and openly. "I beg you" is the same as "I beg you." Paul does not give a cold order, but pleads warmly that they accept the person back again.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about someone who had been disciplined by the community. The person's name is not given, and scholars discuss whether this is the man from 1 Corinthians 5 or another case. What is clear is that the punishment was already enough, and now the person is very sad. Paul wants them to be forgiven and comforted.

When someone admits his mistake and repents, it is not enough to say "I already forgave you." We can show love through actions: a kind word, an invitation, a hug, and so help that person feel again like part of the family.
exp.10:5:
Paul says that perhaps he is not a brilliant speaker ("rude in speech" means plain or unpolished in how he talks), but he does have true knowledge. He adds that he has already made clear to them, in all things and in front of everyone, who he is and what his ministry is like.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were being influenced by some teachers who presented themselves as superior and spoke with great eloquence. Some criticized Paul for the way he spoke. He does not defend himself out of pride, but to protect the church from a different gospel. Scholars debate exactly who those "super-apostles" were, but the context shows that Paul contrasts them with his own sincerity.

Today we can learn not to measure a message by how impressive the speaker is, but by their faithfulness to Christ and his Word. Good character and a simple truth are worth more than elegant words.
exp.3:6:
This verse says that the apostles have a very valuable treasure: the light of the knowledge of God's glory in Jesus Christ. But they carry it in earthen vessels, that is, in fragile bodies, like simple clay jars. The word "vessels" here means the containers that hold the treasure, and the fragility of the human body makes it clear that the strength is not ours. The power that is so great and surpassing comes from God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were used to admiring brilliant speakers. He reminds them that he does not preach himself, but Christ. Right away he speaks of his sufferings: afflictions, persecution, and being cast down. His weaknesses do not hinder the message; rather, they show that God is the one who sustains.

For today: when you feel tired, limited, or flawed, do not hide your weakness or wait until you are perfect in order to serve. Offer God what you are and trust that his power works through you.
exp.10:19:
This verse says that the Corinthians put up with anyone who mistreated them: whoever enslaved them, preyed on them and took advantage of their goods, took something from them, thought himself superior, or even struck them in the face. The phrase "if a man bring you into bondage" means dominating them as servants, and "if a man exalt himself" means setting himself above others.

Paul writes to them with irony, because some teachers who presented themselves as superior to him had arrived in Corinth. Paul feels compelled to boast and speaks foolishly to show that they tolerated those men, yet doubted the one who had served them with love. Scholars debate whether the blow to the face was literal or a picture of humiliation.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we follow. A leader who controls us, uses us, or humiliates us does not reflect Christ. Let us test everything in the light of the Bible and seek humble guides who serve.
exp.1:11:
Paul tells how he came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ. There a door had been opened for him, that is, a good opportunity to proclaim the message. The phrase breaks off here and continues in the next verse.

The one speaking is Paul, writing to the Corinthians after a strained relationship with them. He was deeply worried about how things were going in Corinth and was waiting for news from Titus. So, although there was an opportunity in Troas, he had no peace and went on to Macedonia looking for him.

For today: an open door does not always mean that everything is in order in our hearts. When something troubles us, such as a broken relationship, it is wise to deal with it through prayer and wisdom, trusting that God is still at work.
exp.11:2:
Paul repeats that he knows a person who had an extraordinary experience. He says he does not know whether it happened within the body or outside of it, and that only God knows. "Such a man" means "a man like this." The word "whether" introduces the two possibilities he considers.

Paul speaks indirectly, as if he were talking about someone else, though many understand that he is referring to himself. He is defending himself before some Corinthians who doubted his authority. He does not want to boast, so he speaks of revelations with care and humility. His true pride, he says, lies in his weaknesses.

For today: we do not need to understand everything to trust God. Paul admits simply that there are things he does not know. We can do the same, leave what we do not understand in God's hands, and not use our spiritual experiences to feel superior.
exp.7:12:
Paul makes clear that he does not want others to live at ease while the Corinthians go through hardship. The words "eased" and "burdened" in the verse mean relief or comfort on one side and pressure or difficulty on the other. He is not asking for help that would leave them in need.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to encourage them to finish the offering they had promised for the poor Christians in Judea. He reminds them that God values a sincere willingness and what each person can truly give. His goal is equality: that today some help others, and tomorrow, if needed, the situation be reversed.

For today: give generously, but with wisdom and according to your means. Think of someone close to you who is going through need and help them with something concrete, without neglecting the basics of your own family.
exp.4:14:
This verse says that Christ died for all, and that his death has a purpose: that those who now live should no longer live thinking only of themselves, but for Jesus, who died and rose again for them. The word "that" in the verse refers to this purpose, and "but" introduces the contrast between living for oneself and living for him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry. He says that the love of Christ moves him, and that this love "compels" him, meaning it presses him and guides him with force. Because Christ died for all, those who trust in him share in his death in some way and begin a new life. Some understand "all" as the whole of humanity, others as all believers.

Today, before making a decision, we can ask ourselves: "Is this only for me, or does it honor Christ and serve others?" Living grateful for his love changes our daily priorities.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that the Corinthians already excel in many good things: in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in eagerness and effort, and in their love toward Paul. So Paul encourages them to excel also in this grace, which here refers to generosity in giving.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He speaks to them about the offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He holds up as an example the churches of Macedonia, who gave with great sacrifice. He makes clear that he is not commanding them, but inviting them to show a sincere love.

For today: it is not enough to have good words or good knowledge of God. Ask yourself in what concrete way you can give with joy, according to your means, to help someone who is in need.
exp.0:2:
Paul begins by praising God. He calls Him "God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ," that is, the Father of Jesus. He also calls Him "the Father of mercies," which means that compassion and forgiveness come from Him. And "the God of all comfort": the one who gives encouragement and relief in any situation. "Blessed" here means "praised."

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Corinth, together with Timothy. He had already come through very hard times, and in the verses that follow he speaks of his afflictions. Before explaining his sufferings, he begins by giving thanks to God for having sustained him.

For today: when you go through a difficult moment, draw near to God in prayer and tell Him what you feel. He comforts. Then, look for a way to lovingly accompany someone who is suffering, sharing the comfort that you received.
exp.1:6:
Paul asks the Corinthians to do the opposite of punishing now: to forgive and comfort that person.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a painful moment. Someone caused hurt, and the community gave that person a rebuke by majority. It is not known with certainty who this was or what the exact offense was; scholars interpret it in various ways. What is clear is that the punishment has already done its purpose, and now it is time to restore.

For today: correction should not be the end of the story. If someone has repented and has already been corrected, help them get back on their feet with a kind word, a hug, or an invitation. Forgiving and comforting is also a way of obeying God.
exp.2:6:
Paul says that the law written on tablets of stone, which he calls the "ministration of death," came with glory. Moses' face shone so brightly that the people of Israel could not look steadily at it. That glory, however, was temporary. The word "was" in this verse means "was," and "to be done away" here means to fade away.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry against those who questioned it. He compares the old covenant, based on the law that revealed sin and condemnation, with the new covenant, given by the Spirit who gives life. His argument is that if what came before had glory, what is new has even more.

For today: do not trust in keeping rules to earn God's favor. Ask the Spirit to transform your heart, and live thankful for the grace Christ has given you.
exp.0:13:
The Corinthians have already come to recognize, though only in part, that Paul and his companions are a source of pride for them, and that they are likewise a source of pride for Paul. "Glory" here means a cause for pride or joy. "You have" is the same as "they have," and "you" is the same as "you all." This mutual joy will reach its fullness on the day of the Lord Jesus, when Christ returns and everything is made known.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he had experienced tensions and misunderstandings. Earlier he has defended his sincere conduct and his integrity. Now he reminds them that, despite their doubts, there is a bond of mutual appreciation. Many understand that, by saying "in part," Paul acknowledges that not everyone in Corinth yet saw it this way.

For today: value those who have helped you in your faith and tell them sincerely that you are grateful for their life. Also take care of your relationships in the church, remembering that what we do together will have value before Christ.
exp.5:5:
This verse continues a list of qualities that show how a true servant of God lives. "Pureness" means purity of life; "knowledge" is spiritual understanding; "longsuffering" is patience with people, enduring without giving up; "kindness" is gentle and kind treatment. It also mentions the Holy Ghost and a love "unfeigned," that is, sincere, without hypocrisy.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. Some doubted his authority. For that reason he presents no credentials, but rather his conduct: sufferings, purity, and love. There are different opinions about whether "by the Holy Ghost" refers to the Spirit of God working in him or to a holy spirit, but most understand it as the Spirit of God.

For today: ask yourself whether your love is sincere. This week, serve someone without expecting recognition or applause, and treat them with real patience and kindness.
exp.0:5:
Paul says that his sufferings have a purpose that benefits the Corinthians. If he goes through afflictions, it is so that they may receive consolation and salvation. If he is comforted, that too is for their good. "Health" here means salvation or spiritual well-being. "Effectual" means that this consolation works or becomes effective, and it shows when they endure patiently the same sufferings.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he had had a strained relationship. He explains to them that his suffering as an apostle is not a sign that God has abandoned him. Shortly afterward he recounts a very hard trial he experienced in Asia. He wants them to understand that they are united in suffering and in comfort.

For today: when God comforts you in a difficulty, do not keep that comfort only for yourself. Think of someone who is suffering something similar and offer them your company, a phone call, or a prayer.
exp.10:12:
Paul says that some people who present themselves as apostles are actually false ones. They are "fraudulent workers," that is, deceitful workers who cheat people. "Transforming themselves" means they change their appearance to seem like genuine apostles, sent by Christ, when they are not.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he founded. Teachers had come there who praised themselves and questioned his authority. Paul makes clear that his love for them is real and that he will not change his conduct, so that those teachers have no reason to boast. Right after this he says that Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.

For today: do not be impressed only by appearance, charisma, or a leader's titles. Always compare what they teach with the Bible, and look at whether their life reflects the character of Christ.
exp.11:9:
Paul says that he takes pleasure in his weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, and in distresses, as long as they are for the sake of Christ. In this verse, "weak" means lacking strength, and "strong" means having power. His point is that when he admits his weakness, God's power works in him.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and defending his authority as an apostle against others who boasted of their achievements. Just before this, he tells how he asked three times for God to take away a suffering that he calls a thorn in the flesh, and the Lord answered him: "My grace is sufficient for you." Scholars do not know for certain what that thorn was.

Today, when you feel limited or tired, you do not have to pretend to be strong. You can tell God honestly what you lack and ask him to sustain you by his grace. His help comes right in those moments.
exp.9:2:
Paul says that although he lives in a human body, weak and mortal, he does not fight his battles with human or selfish methods. The word "war" in the verse means to fight as a soldier does. "The flesh" refers to the way of thinking and acting of the world, marked by pride, manipulation, or self-reliance.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some of them accused him of acting out of human interests. They saw him as humble when he was present and bold when he wrote from a distance. He answers that his authority does not come from human tricks. In the verses that follow, he explains that his weapons have divine power.

For today: when you face a conflict, whether in the family, the church, or at work, do not respond with shouting, hints, or manipulation. Pray, speak the truth with respect, and trust that God works better than your pride.
exp.12:11:
Paul asks the believers in Corinth to greet one another with a holy kiss, that is, a greeting kiss that expresses pure, brotherly and sisterly affection. He then adds that all the saints, meaning the believers who are with him, send their greetings to them.

Paul ends this letter, which was harsh in several parts, on a note of peace. He has just urged them to seek unity and joy. In that time, greeting one another with a kiss on the cheek was a common custom. The word "holy" sets it apart as a clean gesture, a sign of family in the faith, not any other kind of affection.

Today the form of the greeting matters less, since it varies from culture to culture, than its spirit. Think of someone in your church with whom there is distance or tension, and greet them with genuine warmth: a hug, a handshake, or a few kind words.
exp.0:6:
Paul says that his hope regarding the Corinthians is steadfast, that is, it does not waver. He is confident that just as they share in the sufferings, they will also share in God's comfort. "Partners" means companions or participants, people who go together through both the good and the hard times.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with whom he had experienced tensions. He speaks to them of his own afflictions and of the comfort he received from God. Soon he will tell them about a very harsh trial he went through in Asia, where he felt he would die. He wants them to know that suffering and comfort go together.

Today, if you are going through a trial because you follow Christ, you are not alone. God comforts you, and that comfort is not only for you: you can share it with others who suffer, accompanying them with prayer, listening, and words of encouragement.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that when a person turns to the Lord, the veil that was covering their understanding is taken away. Here, "turning" means turning toward God, and the veil is a picture of spiritual blindness that keeps a person from seeing the true meaning of the Scriptures.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and recalls that Moses covered his face after speaking with God (Exodus 34). Paul uses that image to say that many of his people read the law of Moses without recognizing that it pointed to Christ. Some understand "the Lord" as Christ, others as God in general, but the sense is very similar.

For today: if there are parts of the Bible you do not understand, come to Christ with humility and ask him for light. Reading Scripture while looking to Jesus opens the understanding and transforms the heart little by little.
exp.6:0:
This verse calls us to cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles, both body and spirit, that is, our conduct and also our thoughts and attitudes. "Filthiness" means dirt or impurity. "Perfecting holiness" means continuing to grow in a life set apart for God, and "the fear of God" is respect and reverence toward Him. We are asked to do this "having therefore these promises."

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth. The promises he refers to are in the previous chapter (6:16-18), where God says He will dwell among His people and be their Father. Then Paul asks them to receive him warmly, since he has wronged no one. Some scholars see here an invitation to separate themselves from the pagan practices of the city.

Today, if God promises us His nearness and His care, we can respond with gratitude. This week, identify one habit or thought that pulls you away from Him and ask Him for help to leave it behind.
exp.1:2:
Paul says he wrote that letter so that he would not arrive in Corinth and find sorrow where he expected joy. He trusted that his joy was also the joy of all of them, meaning that they shared the same desires and rejoiced together.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth, with whom he had a strained relationship. He had had to correct them, and this pained him. He preferred to do it by letter rather than with another painful visit, to give them time to change. Scholars debate which letter this is, but the meaning is clear: he was moved by love, not anger.

For today: when you have to say something hard to someone you love, do it with care and with time, seeking their good and the restoration of the relationship, not winning an argument.
exp.12:2:
Paul says that the Corinthians are asking for proof that Christ speaks through him. He reminds them that Christ is not weak toward them, but powerful among them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which had been corrected several times. Some doubted his authority as an apostle because his presence seemed weak and plain. He warns that he will come a third time and that, if necessary, he will act firmly against those who continue in sin. His words are not from pride, but from pastoral care.

For today: before demanding proof from others, look at how Christ has already been at work in your life. Be humble before correction, because God often uses ordinary people to speak truth to us.
exp.11:8:
Paul tells what the Lord answered when he asked three times that his thorn be taken away: "My grace is enough for you," that is, his undeserved favor and help. The strength that God gives is made complete in weakness, meaning that it reaches its full measure and shows itself whole. That is why Paul gladly boasts in his weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon him.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who doubted his authority and admired other teachers who seemed more impressive. He speaks of an extraordinary revelation and of a "thorn in the flesh." We do not know for certain what it was; a sickness, an opposition, or a personal trial have been suggested, but the text does not say.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. Bring your weariness or your limits to God honestly, and trust that his grace sustains you right there.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that the churches of Macedonia went through a very hard trial, with a great deal of suffering. Even so, their joy overflowed, and their extreme poverty did not keep them from giving generously. The word "generosity" here means sincere openness of heart, and the phrase "they gave abundantly" means that they gave a great deal, even though they had very little.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to take part in a collection for the needy Christians in Jerusalem. To motivate them, he holds up the Macedonians as an example (including those in Philippi and Thessalonica). Paul attributes that generosity to the grace of God, not to their wealth.

For today: do not wait until you have plenty to be generous. The joy that comes from God can move your heart to share, even when you have little, even in difficult times.
exp.10:22:
Paul asks whether the other teachers are ministers of Christ, and he clarifies that he speaks as a foolish man would. Even so, he claims that he is more. He mentions more labors, beatings beyond measure, more imprisonments, and many times he was close to death.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some teachers boasted of being superior and questioned his authority. He compares himself with them, but he does so with irony and reluctance, calling it foolishness. He does not boast of successes but of sufferings, to show that his service to Christ was real and costly.

For today: let us not measure Christian service by how impressive or successful it looks, but by faithfulness, love, and humble self-giving. When faced with someone who boasts a great deal, let us look for the fruit and character of Christ.
exp.11:3:
This verse says that the man was "caught up", that is, carried away suddenly and forcibly, into paradise. There he heard unspeakable words, things that cannot be told or that a person is not allowed to repeat.

The apostle Paul is speaking. He almost certainly means himself, though he tells it as if he were speaking of another person. He does this because some in Corinth boasted of visions and spiritual superiority, and he answers with humility. Whether it happened in the body or outside of it, he himself does not know. Then he says he would rather boast of his weaknesses.

For today: you do not need extraordinary experiences to be valued before God. Paul chose to keep silent and not boast. Try to keep humility in your faith, trusting more in God's grace than in your spiritual experiences.
exp.0:9:
He delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver us; in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us. This verse says that God rescued Paul and his companions from a danger of death so great that he continues to do so, and that they trust he will do it again.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He tells them that in Asia they went through a trial so severe that they nearly gave up hope of living. We do not know exactly what that affliction was; various ideas have been proposed, but the text does not make it clear. Paul explains that this experience taught them not to trust in themselves, but in God, who raises the dead. He also asks them to pray for them.

For today: when you remember how God sustained you through past trials, let that strengthen your trust for what lies ahead. Write down those times and give thanks for them, and do not stop asking other believers for prayer.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that the message of Christ, which Paul and his companions proclaim, is perceived in two ways. For those who reject it, it is like a smell that leads to death; for those who receive it, it is a fragrance that leads to life. Then Paul asks: "who is sufficient for these things?", that is, who is qualified for a task so serious?

Paul writes to the Corinthians and speaks about his ministry. He uses the image of a victorious parade, where incense is smelled everywhere. Some understand this as a reference to Roman parades, though not everyone agrees. In the following verse, he answers that he does not preach for gain, but with sincerity before God.

For today: when you share your faith, do not depend on your own ability. Speak with honesty and trust that God is the one who opens hearts, even though some respond well and others do not.
exp.3:12:
Paul says that he and his companions have the same spirit of faith that the psalmist had. The psalmist wrote: "I believed, and therefore have I spoken" (Psalm 116:10). Paul says that because they believe, they also speak.

Paul writes to the Corinthians in the middle of suffering and danger for preaching Christ. He has just said that they are given over to death for Jesus. Even so, their faith does not go out, and for that reason they keep proclaiming the gospel. Their hope is that God, who raised Jesus, will also raise them. Some scholars note that Paul quotes the psalm according to the ancient Greek version.

For today: if you truly believe in Jesus, your faith can come out in words. Even when you go through trials, take courage to speak simply of what God has done in you, with a friend, your family, or in prayer.
exp.4:9:
It says that all of us, without exception, will have to appear before the judgment seat of Christ. The verse's "must" is the word for what is necessary, and the verse's "appear" means that we must present ourselves there. There each person will receive according to what they did while living in the body, whether good or bad. Christians understand this moment in different ways, but the text speaks of a real accounting.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth. He had just been talking about his desire to be with the Lord and to please him, whether in this life or the next. He was also defending the sincerity of his ministry against those who criticized him and looked only at outward appearances.

For today: live each day with the awareness that Christ sees your motives, not just your appearances. Before deciding something, ask yourself: "Is this pleasing to the Lord?" Do it with confidence and reverence, not with fear.
exp.0:12:
Paul says that his letters contain nothing hidden or different from what the Corinthians already read and understand. The phrase "or also acknowledge" means "or accept as true." He hopes they will keep understanding it to the end, that is, until Christ returns or until the end of his relationship with them.

Paul is writing to a church where some doubted his sincerity, since he had changed his travel plans. Earlier he said he had acted with "simplicity and godly sincerity." Here he argues that his words are clear and consistent, without double intentions. Some scholars see a wordplay in the Greek between "read" and "acknowledge," but that is an interpretation.

For today: make sure your words and your actions match. Speak with clarity and honesty in your family, your work, and your church, so that those who know you find no hidden surprises in your character.
exp.6:4:
He says that when Paul and his companions arrived in Macedonia, they had no rest. Their flesh here refers to their whole being, body and spirit. They were troubled, that is, under heavy pressure. Outside there were conflicts, which means struggles or arguments, and inside they felt fears, that is, dread and worry. The phrase "came into" would be written "came to" today.

Paul is speaking, writing to the Corinthians. He tells them honestly how hard his journey was while he waited for news from them. He had sent Titus and was anxious about how things would go for them. The next verse shows that God comforted him with Titus's arrival and his good news.

For today: you do not need to pretend to be strong. Paul admitted his fears with honesty. You can bring God your struggles from outside and your fears from within, and also let other believers be the means of comfort that He sends you.
exp.3:14:
Paul says that everything he endures, he endures for the sake of the Corinthians. His aim is that God's grace reach more and more people, so that the thanksgiving offered to God grows as well, and God is glorified.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with which he had experienced tensions. He defends his ministry and explains that his sufferings do not defeat him, because he trusts in the resurrection. His difficulties serve so that others may know the gospel and receive the grace of God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we see our difficulties only as a burden or also as an opportunity. When we serve with patience and faith, even in the midst of weariness, God can use us to bless others. And every blessing received is one more reason to give thanks.
exp.0:16:
Paul asks two questions. He asks whether, in changing his travel plans, he acted with "lightness," that is, with carelessness or a lack of seriousness. And whether he decides things "according to the flesh," that is, out of human convenience, so that he would say "Yes" and "No" at the same time.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians. He had planned to visit them twice, but he did not do it the way he had intended. Some in Corinth were probably accusing him of being inconstant and unreliable. He maintains that his changes did not come from a double heart. The verses that follow connect this with the faithfulness of God and of Christ.

For today: when you have to change a plan or cannot keep what you promised, explain your reasons with humility and sincerity. Work to make your word trustworthy, thinking before you promise and not out of simple convenience.
exp.7:18:
He says that the brother known for his service in the gospel was not sent by Paul alone, but chosen by the churches to travel with them. His task was to carry the offering, which Paul and his team were administering to honor the Lord and to show the readiness of the Corinthians.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to encourage them to finish a collection for the believers in need in Jerusalem. He explains that Titus and another brother will go to help. The verse does not say with certainty who this brother is; several names have been proposed, but the Bible does not make it clear.

For today: handle the church's money with transparency and with the help of several trustworthy people. In this way we protect our witness and give glory to God.
exp.10:23:
It says that Paul received five times from the Jews the punishment of thirty-nine lashes. "Forty stripes save one" means thirty-nine blows of the whip. In total there were 195 blows, and that was only on these five occasions.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth. Some false teachers were boasting of their credentials and criticizing Paul. He, reluctantly, and saying that he speaks as a fool, lists his sufferings for Christ. Many believe he held back at forty so as not to go beyond the limit of the law (Deuteronomy 25:3), although the Bible does not explain this here.

For today: true service to God is not measured by success or appearance, but by faithfulness in the midst of difficulties. When you serve with love and it costs you, remember that God sees what others do not see.
exp.1:1:
He says that if Paul makes the Corinthians sad, who will make him glad? Only the very people he had made sad. The word "sorry" in the verse means causing sadness or pain. Here, the word "then" means "in that case" or "afterward." Paul shows that his joy and theirs are closely bound together.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a tense and painful relationship. He had to correct them firmly.
