For that reason he decided not to make another painful visit, but to write to them first, so that the resolving of the problems would allow a joyful visit. Some scholars think he is referring to an earlier letter; others hold different views, and the Bible does not settle the question completely.

For today: when you have to correct someone, do it with love and with their good in mind, not to wound. And remember that in the church and in the family joy is shared, and that a sincere correction can prepare the way for comfort and restoration.
exp.6:6:
Paul says that Titus encouraged him not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort Titus himself had received from them. Titus told him that the Corinthians longed for him, that they grieved over what had happened, and that they cared deeply for Paul. All of this gave him even more joy. "Mourning" means weeping, and "fervent mind" means sincere and burning concern.

Paul writes from Macedonia, weary from pressures from outside and fears from within. Earlier he had sent them a strong letter to correct them, and he waited anxiously for their response. Titus came back with good news: the church responded with repentance and affection toward him.

For today: God often comforts us through other people. We can be like Titus, bringing a word of encouragement to someone who is suffering. We can also receive correction humbly from those who love us, because it can bring healing and reconciliation.
exp.11:4:
He says that Paul is willing to boast about that certain man who was taken up to paradise. But about himself he will not boast of anything, except his weaknesses, meaning his frailties and limitations. To boast means to take pride in something or to show off.

Paul speaks to the Corinthians, who were impressed by teachers who bragged about visions and power. To defend his ministry, Paul recounts this experience in the third person, and almost everyone thinks he is referring to himself, though he does not say so openly. Then he mentions his thorn, which kept him humble. We do not know for certain what it was.

Today we can learn not to base our worth on impressive achievements or spiritual experiences. Simply acknowledging our weaknesses keeps us humble and shows that strength comes from God.
exp.11:18:
Paul asks them whether they still think he is defending himself before them. He makes clear that he does not speak to please people, but with a clear conscience before God, "in Christ." He says that everything he has said, dear church, has a purpose: to build you up, that is, to strengthen you in the faith.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, some of whom had turned against him, accusing him of acting with deceit, even in how he handled money. He recalls that Titus and the brother he sent acted with honesty. His defense does not seek his own pride, but their good before he visits them again.

For today: when you correct or advise someone, examine your motive. Ask yourself whether you are speaking to win an argument or to help that person grow, and speak with sincerity before God.
exp.1:12:
He says that Paul had no peace in his heart because he did not find Titus, whom he calls "my brother." So he said goodbye to the people in Troas and went on to Macedonia.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, with whom he had had a strained relationship. He had sent Titus to learn how they had received his earlier letter, and he hoped to meet him in Troas. Although there was an open door there for preaching, his concern for the church in Corinth weighed more heavily. Commentators debate how long he stayed in Troas, but the text does not make this clear.

God is concerned not only with our tasks but also with people and relationships. If something troubles you about someone you love, do not ignore it: pray, seek reconciliation, and take the necessary step.
exp.6:8:
Paul says that he now rejoices, but not because the Corinthians felt sorrow. He rejoices because that sorrow led them to change their course. The word "sorrowed" means being grieved or deeply pained. It was a sorrow "after a godly manner," meaning the kind that God uses for good. In this way they lost nothing because of the correction Paul gave them.

Paul had written them a strong letter to correct them, and that caused them pain. Later Titus brought him good news: the church had responded with seriousness and a desire to amend their ways. That is why Paul writes to them relieved. He makes clear that his joy is not in having hurt them, but in the fruit that came afterward.

For today: when someone corrects you with love, do not become defensive right away. Ask yourself before God whether there is something you need to change. The sorrow that leads you back to God heals; it does not destroy.
exp.5:17:
It says that God promises to be a Father to his people, and that they will be his sons and daughters. "Almighty Lord" is a title that stresses his total power. The old spellings of the words in the source are no longer used; today the sentence would read "unto you" and "sons and daughters" as they appear in the verse above.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, who lived surrounded by idolatry. He asks them not to join in practices that contradict their faith. To support this, he gathers several phrases from the Old Testament, and this verse seems to draw ideas from texts such as 2 Samuel 7:14 and Isaiah 43:6. Some scholars see here a loose quotation rather than an exact one. The promise follows the invitation to separate from what is impure.

Today, when you decide to step away from something that harms your faith, you are not alone. God receives you as a father receives his children. Obey with confidence in his care.
exp.0:10:
Paul tells the Corinthians that they too are working together with him through prayer. The "gift" is the favor or kindness of God, which here refers to God delivering him from a deadly danger. The phrase "by the means of many persons" means that this favor came because of the prayers of many people. The result is that many will give thanks to God for him.

Paul writes from a situation of great distress, which he mentions in the verses before, where he felt he was going to die. It is not known for certain exactly what it was, and scholars interpret it in several ways. He confesses that he learned to rely only on God, who raises the dead, and he asks the church to keep praying.

For today: our prayer for others truly matters. Today you can pray for a pastor, a missionary, or a friend in trouble, and then rejoice and give thanks to God when he answers.
exp.4:18:
It says that God, through Christ, was bringing humanity back to himself. "Reconciling" means making friends again with those who had been separated. "Not counting their sins against them" means that God does not charge people for their wrongs or hold them accountable for their guilt. And God has entrusted us with sharing this message with others. The word "unto himself" simply means "to himself."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, with whom he had a difficult relationship. He defends his ministry and reminds them that everything begins with God, not with human effort. The verses that follow describe him as an ambassador: someone who speaks on behalf of another and pleads with people to accept peace with God.

For today: if God has already taken the step toward us, we can live without fear or shame. We can also offer that same forgiveness to others, with kind words and patience, whether in the family, at work, or with a friend we have drifted away from.
exp.7:3:
Paul tells that the believers of Macedonia urged him again and again to accept their gift. For them, giving was a privilege, a favor they were grateful to receive. Taking part in that help is what the verse calls "the fellowship of the ministering," and "the saints" are the Christians in need in Jerusalem.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish their offering. He holds up the churches of Macedonia as an example: they lived in affliction and poverty, yet they gave with joy. They themselves asked for the favor of taking part, without anyone forcing them.

Giving is not only an obligation; it can also be a privilege. This week, think of a specific need of a brother or sister or of your church, and give with joy whatever you can, even if it is little. God looks at the heart with which we give.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that when we receive our heavenly dwelling, we will be found "clothed" and not "naked." Paul uses the image of clothing to speak about the body. Being "naked" suggests being without a body, and being "clothed" refers to having the new body that God gives. Some translators read the phrase as "if indeed," and scholars debate the exact meaning of the wording.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He speaks to them of the hope of the resurrection in the midst of suffering and the frailty of present life. He compares the current body to a tent and the future to an eternal house. Interpreters differ on whether he is speaking of an intermediate state after death, but his confidence in God is clear.

Today, when the body grows tired or life hurts, we can rest in the fact that God is preparing something better for us. Let us live with hope, trusting in the Spirit he gave us as a guarantee.
exp.0:15:
This verse explains the travel plan Paul had. He wanted to visit the Corinthians first, then go on to Macedonia, then return to Corinth and, from there, be sent on his way toward Judea. The phrase "to pass by you into Macedonia" means going on toward Macedonia, and "to be brought on my way" means that they would help him return or continue on his journey.

Paul writes this letter to a church that was criticizing him because he had changed his plans. Some accused him of being unstable or of not speaking in earnest. That is why he reminds them of his original intention: to visit them twice so that they would be encouraged. In the verses that follow, he argues that his word is sincere and trustworthy.

For today: when you have to change a plan, explain your reasons with humility and honesty. And when someone changes their plans, do not assume the worst right away. Clear and kind communication helps protect trust.
exp.7:5:
He says that Paul and his companions encouraged Titus to finish the work he had already started among the Corinthians. "Grace" here refers to the generous offering to help other believers. "Exhorted" means to encourage earnestly, and "finish" means to complete it.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. The Christians of Macedonia, though they were poor, had given with joy for the needy saints in Jerusalem. Titus had already begun this collection in Corinth, and Paul wants them now to bring it to completion. He does not command it, but invites them warmly to show a sincere love.

For today: if you have started something good, such as helping someone or supporting a cause, do not leave it half-done. Ask God for steadiness, and finish it with joy and sincere love.
exp.11:12:
Paul asks them, with irony, in what way they were treated worse than the other churches. The only difference, he says, is that he did not burden them, meaning he did not ask them for money for his support. Then he says, "Forgive me this wrong," which is to say, "Forgive me this offense." He says it with an ironic tone, like someone apologizing for having done them a favor.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his authority as an apostle against critics who looked down on him. He feels uncomfortable having to speak about himself, and for that reason he says that he has become a fool. Some think his decision not to charge them was disapproved of by some people in Corinth, but the text does not fully explain this.

Today we can learn that serving others out of love sometimes means giving up our own rights. We also learn not to take offense at someone who serves us generously, nor to measure their affection by what it costs us.
exp.8:2:
Paul says that he sent some brothers to Corinth so that what he has said with pride about them in this matter would not turn out empty. "Glory" here means a reason for pride, and "vain" means empty or without foundation. "Ready" means prepared, set. He wants them to be ready, just as he had already said.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about the collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem (the "saints"). He had spoken well of them to the Macedonians, and now he sends Titus and other brothers to help them complete what they had promised. He did not want his praise to end in shame.

For today: if we have promised to help someone, let us follow through with order and joy. Making a concrete plan, instead of leaving it to the last minute, honors God and protects our witness.
exp.2:3:
Paul says he has a firm confidence, and that he has this confidence "through Christ" before God. He is not talking about self-assurance, but about a certainty that comes through Jesus. The phrase "to God-ward" means "before God" or "in his presence."

Paul is writing to believers in Corinth. Some were questioning his authority and asking for letters of recommendation. He answers that the proof of his ministry is the people themselves: lives changed by the Spirit. That fruit encourages him to speak with confidence. In the verses that follow, he clarifies that his ability comes from God, not from himself.

For today: when you feel incapable or unsure about what God has entrusted to you, remember that your confidence rests not on your talents but on Christ. Serve with humility and courage, because God is the one who gives the ability.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that the help the Corinthians are preparing does not only meet the needs of the believers who are poor, who are called here "the saints." It also leads many people to give thanks to God. The phrase "administration of this service" refers to the act of delivering this help. "Supplieth" means that it fills what is lacking. "Thanksgivings" are expressions of gratitude.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to complete an offering for the Christians in need in Jerusalem. Many understand that there was scarcity there, although the text does not give all the details. Paul wants them to give with joy and to see that their generosity has a greater purpose: that God be honored.

For today: when you help someone in need, do it simply and with trust in God. Your help meets a need, but it can also lead others to thank God.
exp.0:17:
Paul says that God, who is faithful, knows that what he told the Corinthians was not a "yes" and a "no" at the same time. That is, his word was not doubtful or changeable.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He had changed his travel plans, and some accused him of being inconstant and of speaking lightly, "according to the flesh," that is, out of human convenience. He defends his sincerity and calls God as witness. Then he connects his word with the faithfulness of Christ, in whom God fulfills his promises.

For today: work to make your word trustworthy. Keep what you promise and, if you truly must change a plan, explain the reasons with honesty and humility.
exp.9:16:
It says that if someone wants to boast or take pride in something, they should do so in what God is and has done, not in themselves. "Boast" means to show pride or take pleasure in something. "Let him glory" is the command form: "let him boast."

The apostle Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. Some there were bragging and comparing themselves to the leaders, and they questioned Paul's authority. He answers that he does not boast about the work of others, but hopes that their faith will grow and that the gospel will reach new places. This verse sums up a phrase Paul takes from the ancient Scriptures (probably Jeremiah 9:24).

When you accomplish something, whether at work, in your studies, or in service, give thanks to God and recognize that He gave you the strength and the opportunities. In this way you avoid pride and also envy toward others.
exp.2:17:
It says that all believers, with unveiled faces, behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror. As we look at him, the Spirit gradually changes us, so that we become more and more like Jesus.

The phrase "from glory to glory" means from one level of growth to another, step by step.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and compares the old covenant with the new. He recalls that Moses covered his face with a veil, and he says that this veil is taken away when someone turns to the Lord. Now there is freedom to draw near to God. Some understand the mirror as an imperfect reflection; others understand it as the place where we are transformed.

For today: spend a few minutes each day looking at Christ in his Word and in prayer, without fear or excuses. Ask the Spirit to change you, and be patient: transformation is a process, not a single moment.
exp.8:4:
Paul says he thought it necessary to ask the brothers (Titus and his companions) to visit the Corinthians first. They were to help the church get ready the gift it had already promised. The word "ready" in the verse above means prepared in advance. "Stinginess" means grudging giving, giving reluctantly and only the minimum. Paul wants the gift to be a generous blessing, not something pulled out of them by force.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the gift for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. The Corinthians had promised it earlier, and Paul had spoken well of them to the Macedonians. He did not want them to arrive with the Corinthians and find nothing ready, leaving everyone embarrassed.

For today: if God puts it on your heart to help someone or support your church, decide early and prepare your help calmly. That way you can give with joy, without last-minute pressure.
exp.12:1:
Paul reminds them of something he had already warned them about: when he comes to Corinth for the third time, he will not spare those who sinned earlier or the others who keep on in the same way. He says it as if he were present, although he is writing from a distance.

Paul writes to a church that had questioned his authority. Some doubted that Christ spoke through him. That is why he warns them firmly that he does not want to catch them by surprise: he prefers that they put things right before he arrives. Some scholars think he has a specific apostolic discipline in mind; the text does not give details.

For today: if there is something in your life that God has shown you, do not wait for the correction to arrive. Acknowledge it and put it right now, with humility, while there is still time.
exp.10:11:
Paul says he will keep doing what he has been doing: preaching to the Corinthians without charging them. In this way he removes the opportunity from those who look for one. He wants them to be found just like him in the very thing they boast about.

Paul speaks to the church in Corinth. He has served without receiving support from them, and some rival teachers used this to question his love and his authority. Paul states that his motive is love for them, and that none of this comes from contempt. He then calls those men false apostles. Scholars debate the exact details of what they intended, but the text shows that Paul did not want to give them any pretext.

For today: let us make sure that the way we serve is clear and honest, even when it costs us. Sometimes it is worth giving up a right so that the gospel is not hindered or open to suspicion.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that the old covenant, the law given through Moses, had glory, but it was temporary. "That which is passing away" refers to that which was coming to an end. By contrast, the new covenant, "that which remains," has a greater glory because it lasts forever. "Will be in glory" means that it will have abundant glory.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth. Some teachers were pulling them back toward the law of Moses. Paul shows them that the law was good and glorious, but the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness in Christ surpasses it. Interpreters agree on the general idea, although they debate some details about how it applies to the law.

For today: do not live your faith as a list of requirements to earn God's favor. Rest in what Christ has already done, and let his Spirit transform you little by little.
exp.5:6:
It says that Paul and his companions show themselves to be true servants of God in three ways: they speak the truth, they live with the power of God, and they use the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left. That means they are protected and equipped on every side, both to attack and to defend, with an upright life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. Some doubted his authority. For that reason he presents his ministry as evidence: he endures beatings and imprisonment, yet he remains steadfast. His character and the power of God, not fame, are his credentials.

For today: in trials, defend your faith with an honest and just life rather than with arguments. Before answering a criticism, ask yourself whether your words are true and whether your actions reflect God. Ask him for his strength to do so.
exp.5:16:
This verse calls believers to come out from among certain people or practices, to live set apart, and not to touch what is "unclean," that is, whatever defiles. God promises, "I will receive you," meaning he will welcome them as his own. The words "come out" and "be separate" are commands in the plural, addressed to the whole church.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were surrounded by idols and a pagan culture. He has just said that they are the temple of the living God, and that Christ and Belial (a name for evil) cannot go together. Using words taken from the Old Testament, Paul reminds them that God wants a people of his own. The next verse promises that God will be their Father.

Today we can ask ourselves what habit, relationship, or influence pulls us away from God. This is not about looking down on people, but about setting wise boundaries to guard our faith, trusting that the Father receives us with love.
exp.9:4:
This verse speaks of tearing down arguments and every proud thing that rises up against the knowledge of God. It also says that every thought must be brought captive, that is, made subject, to the obedience of Christ.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his authority as an apostle against those who criticized him and judged him by appearances. He explains that his struggle is not carried on with human methods, but with the power of God. The weapons he speaks of are a figure for truth, prayer and testimony, not for violence.

For today: when a thought of pride, doubt or resentment arises, pause and compare it with what Jesus teaches. Bring it to Christ in prayer and choose to obey him, even though at first it may be hard.
exp.7:15:
He says that Paul thanks God because God put into Titus's heart the same care and earnestness that Paul has for the Corinthians. The word "earnest" means eager and sincere concern, a real desire to help.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth to encourage them to finish their offering for the poor Christians in Judea. He had already spoken about generosity and about fairness between the churches. Now he introduces Titus, who would carry this letter and help complete the collection. Paul recognizes that this care for them comes from God.

For today: when you see someone serving with love and dedication, thank God for that person. And ask him to also give you a heart attentive to the needs of others, so that you help with sincerity and not only out of obligation.
exp.3:2:
Paul says that if someone does not understand the gospel he preaches, it is because it is hidden from them, as if covered by a veil. Hidden here means covered or concealed. The words "those who are lost" refer to people who are walking on a path far from God and have not yet believed.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth and defends the honesty of his ministry. He says he does not deceive or change the message. Even so, some do not accept it. He explains that the problem does not lie in the message, and the following verse speaks of a spiritual blindness that keeps people from seeing the light of Christ.

For today: when you share your faith, be honest and clear, without manipulating anyone. If someone does not understand, do not become discouraged or feel guilty. Pray for that person, because only God can open the eyes of the heart.
exp.6:2:
Paul makes clear to them that his earlier words were not an accusation. He tells them that he carries them so deep in his heart that their bond would not be broken, not even in death or in life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a strained relationship. He asks them to receive him again with confidence, because he has not wronged anyone. He had corrected them firmly before, and now he wants them to know that he did it out of love and not out of anger. The verses that follow show his relief and his joy over them.

For today: when you have to correct someone, make clear that you do it because you value them. A correction given with love heals; one given with contempt wounds. Guard your words and your attitude.
exp.1:3:
Paul says he wrote a very firm letter, but he did it with great pain and in tears. "Tribulation" and "anguish of heart" speak of a deep sorrow. "Grieved" means saddened. His purpose was not to hurt them, but to let them know how much he loves them.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a conflict with them. He had sent them a firm letter to correct a serious matter. Many scholars think that letter is different from 1 Corinthians, though there is no complete certainty. Now he wants them to understand that his correction came from love, and he desires to come back to them with joy, not with more sadness.

For today: when you need to correct someone, do it with truth, but also with tenderness and a sincere desire for their good. And when someone corrects you in love, try to see their heart behind the hard words.
exp.10:8:
Paul reminds them that when he was in Corinth and was in need, he did not ask them for help and was not a burden to them. The brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what he lacked. Paul's words here refer to being a trouble or a financial weight to others. He was careful about this then, and he says he will continue to be.

Paul writes to a church where some questioned his authority, and other teachers presented themselves as superior. He explains that he preached the gospel without charging them, so as not to give them any reason for criticism. When he says he "robbed" other churches, he uses a painful exaggeration: other communities supported him while he served in Corinth.

Today we can serve others generously and take care that our decisions do not hinder the gospel. Sometimes it is good to give up a legitimate right out of love, but always with wisdom and without boasting.
exp.2:9:
It says that the law given at Sinai, which did have glory, now barely shines when it is compared with the much greater glory of the new covenant.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and defends his ministry against those who questioned it. He compares the ministry of Moses, the law written on stone, with the ministry of the Spirit, which gives life and righteousness in Christ. He does not say the law was bad; he says its glory was temporary and prepared the way for something greater.

For today: do not live your faith as a list of rules to keep. Trust in what Christ has already done, and let the Spirit transform you, with gratitude and without fear.
exp.7:21:
Paul says that he is sending, along with Titus and the other brother, a third brother, whose name he does not mention. Paul has seen him work with real commitment many times (the word for a careful, dedicated worker is what the verse calls "diligent"). Now he sees him with even more eagerness, because Paul has great confidence in the Corinthians.

Paul is organizing the collection for the poor believers in Judea. To avoid suspicion about how the money is handled, he sends a team of trustworthy people. We do not know for certain who this brother is; some have proposed names, but the text does not say.

Today, when we manage church resources or help others, let us do things with order and openness. Working as a team and being accountable to one another is not distrust; it is a way of caring for our witness and for the name of Christ.
exp.12:12:
This verse is a closing blessing. Paul wishes the Corinthians to receive the grace (the undeserved favor) of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, that is, the communion or companionship that the Spirit gives.

Paul closes a strong letter, in which he corrects a divided church and was questioned about his authority. Even so, he ends with peace and affection. He mentions the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together, one of the clearest blessings in the New Testament regarding the Trinity.

For today: before ending a difficult conversation at home, at church, or at work, bless the other person. Ask that God give them grace, love, and communion, even if you do not yet agree on everything.
exp.10:14:
It says that we should not be surprised if the servants of Satan disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. They "transform themselves," that is, they change their outward appearance to look like something they are not. And the phrase "their end will match their works" means that in the end they will receive what they deserve for what they did, not for how they looked.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and he is defending his ministry. Some preachers came calling themselves apostles and discredited Paul. He calls them false because they deceived the church with an appearance of godliness. Many scholars see here a serious warning about who teaches and how they live.

Today it is not enough for someone to speak well or seem pious. Let us compare what they teach with the Bible and look at their fruit: humility, truth, and love for Christ.
exp.8:6:
The verse says that each person should give according to what they have decided in their heart, and not with sadness or out of obligation. The reason is that God loves the one who gives with joy. The word "dador" in the verse refers to the giver, and the word "purposeth" in the verse means that the decision was made beforehand.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had promised an offering to help the poor believers, whom many understand to be those in Jerusalem. He reminds them to give generously and not stingily. He wants their gift to be voluntary and not a last-minute pressure.

For today: before you give, pray and calmly decide how much you can give. That way your offering comes from a grateful heart and not from guilt, pressure, or habit.
exp.1:5:
It says that for that person, the punishment he received from the majority is already enough, or sufficient. Paul says it has already been enough.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after an earlier letter, written with tears, in which he asked them to correct someone who had caused pain. The man's name is not given here, nor his exact offense, and scholars do not agree on who he was. Most of the church had already corrected him, and Paul asks them now to forgive him and comfort him.

For today: correction should aim to restore, not to humiliate forever. If someone has repented and has already faced the consequences, offer him forgiveness, support, and an open door to walk again with the community.
exp.8:0:
Paul says there is no need to write to them about the "ministering to the saints," that is, the help or gift for believers in need. The phrase "it is superfluous for me to write to you" means it would be pointless for him to write, because they already know about the matter.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. In the previous chapter he spoke of this collection, which many understand as help for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. Now he wants to encourage them tactfully, acknowledging their willingness, so that they finish what they started. The details of how the offering was organized are known only in part from the text.

For today: when someone already has a good willingness to help, it is wise to encourage them with kindness rather than pressure. And if we have promised to help someone, let us ask God for steadiness to carry it out with joy and order.
exp.10:24:
Paul lists some of the sufferings he endured for preaching Christ. He was beaten with rods three times, a punishment carried out by Roman authorities. He was stoned once. He suffered three shipwrecks, and he spent a night and a day in the deep sea, that is, in the middle of the waters, probably floating after a shipwreck, although the text gives no further details.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. Some proud teachers criticized him and boasted of their achievements. So Paul, with a certain irony, speaks as though he were a fool and boasts, but not of successes; he boasts of his weaknesses and of what he suffered in serving.

For today: serving God is not always easy or comfortable. When you go through hardships for doing good, remember that God sustains those who serve him, and that his strength is most evident when we feel weak.
exp.5:14:
This verse asks two questions to show that Christ and Belial cannot walk together. "Concord" means agreement or harmony. "Belial" is a name used to speak of wickedness and, here, of Satan. "Believer" is the one who trusts in Christ, and "infidel" is the one who does not. The implied answer is: none.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whom he treats with affection as his children. He asks them not to be "unequally yoked" (a shared burden, like two oxen tied together) with unbelievers. Interpreters debate whether he means mainly idolatry, marriage, or partnerships in general, and perhaps all of these.

Today, before we commit to a partnership, a relationship, or a cause, let us ask whether we will be able to remain faithful to Christ. That does not mean looking down on anyone: we still love and serve everyone.
exp.4:19:
Paul says that believers are ambassadors of Christ. An ambassador represents a king and speaks in his name. So it is as if God himself were inviting people through them. "Beseech" means to ask earnestly and tenderly. The sentence that explains "reconcile" is removed here, since the reader's verse does not use that word in the explained sense; instead, the meaning is that you should return to peace with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, with whom he had a difficult relationship. Shortly before, he explained that God had already taken the first step: in Christ he did not count people's sins against them. Now Paul describes his mission: to proclaim that message of peace. Some think he also calls the Corinthians to return to God; others see here above all a call to those who do not yet believe.

For today: if God has reconciled us to himself, we can invite others with humility and love, without boasting or condemning. Think of someone close to you and ask God for an opportunity to share his love with simple words.
exp.9:6:
Paul tells the Corinthians that they are judging only by what meets the eye. He then points out that if anyone feels confident that he belongs to Christ, he should recognize that Paul and his companions belong to Christ too.

Paul writes to a church where some people criticized him and doubted his authority, perhaps because of his appearance or his way of speaking. He answers them firmly but with affection. His authority comes from Christ and seeks to build up the church, not tear it down. Interpreters do not fully agree on who these critics were, but the complaint is clear.

Today, before judging someone by their appearance, their style, or the way they speak, stop and ask what is in their heart and their faith. Christ unites those who belong to him, even when they look very different.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that Paul and his companions serve God both when they are honored and when they are despised. It explains that "infamy" is bad reputation and "good name" is a good reputation, though those words are not in the verse you are reading. They are accused of being deceivers, that is, liars or charlatans, but they are truly genuine people, sincere and honest.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some questioned his authority and his honesty. In this passage he describes what true ministry is like: it goes through suffering and criticism, yet remains faithful. Paul does not defend himself with pride, but shows his character and his devotion to Christ.

For today: do not let applause puff you up, nor let unfair criticism sink you. Seek to live with integrity before God. If you are misunderstood, remain sincere and kind, trusting that God knows your heart.
exp.1:0:
Paul says he made a personal decision: not to visit the Corinthians again in sorrow, that is, in an atmosphere of pain and reproach. "I determined this with myself" in the King James wording expresses the same idea of a private resolve made within himself.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, whom he loved despite the conflicts. He had earlier sent them a firm letter to correct them, and he did not want another visit to become a new, painful confrontation. Some scholars think there was a difficult earlier visit, although the text does not say so with complete clarity. What is clear is his desire that his relationship with them be strengthened and that his joy be shared.

Today we can learn to correct others with love and wisdom. Before confronting someone, it is good to pray, to choose the right moment, and to seek restoration, not merely to be right.
exp.9:7:
Paul says that, even if he boasts a little more about the authority the Lord gave him, he will not be ashamed. That authority has a clear purpose: to build up the faith of the Corinthians, not to tear them down. Paul's own word for boasting, which the verse renders as boast, means to take pride in something.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some criticized him and doubted his authority as an apostle. They said his letters were strong, but that in person he was weak. Paul defends his calling without attacking for the sake of it, and makes clear that his goal is to help them grow, even when he has to correct them.

For today: if you have any responsibility, whether in the family, the church, or at work, use it to lift others up and not to humiliate them. Correct firmly when necessary, but with the desire that the person grows.
exp.10:15:
Paul asks that no one think he is a fool. But if they do think so, then let them receive him even as a fool, so that he too may boast a little.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, who were being influenced by false apostles who presented themselves as superior. To show who the true servant of Christ was, Paul finds himself forced to boast, something that makes him uncomfortable. He does it with irony, and in the verses that follow he admits that he is not speaking as the Lord would have him speak, but as one who is out of his mind.

For today: do not be impressed only by the one who speaks well or boasts much. Always compare what you hear with the Word and with the character of Christ. And if at some point you must defend your testimony, do it with humility and without pride.
exp.3:11:
Paul says that he and his companions are going through suffering and danger, a kind of daily dying, and that this brings life to the Corinthians. The word "worketh" means "is active" or "takes effect." The sufferings of the messenger serve so that others receive life.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church with which he had a difficult relationship. He reminds them that preaching the gospel costs him a great deal: persecution, exhaustion, and the risk of dying. But he keeps going with faith, trusting that God, who raised Jesus, will also raise all of them. Some understand "life" as spiritual life; others also include the hope of the resurrection.

For today: serve others even when it costs you. A mother who stays up late, a patient teacher, or a volunteer who gives their time can be channels of life for others. Today, make one concrete gesture of giving for someone, trusting that God will bring fruit.
exp.7:2:
Paul says that the churches of Macedonia gave of their own accord, that is, by their own willingness, with no one forcing them. He says they gave according to what they could, and even beyond their ability, more than seemed possible. Paul adds: "I bear record," as a direct witness to what he saw.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians about the collection for believers in need, probably those in Jerusalem. He holds up the Macedonians as an example; they lived in affliction and poverty, yet they gave with joy. He does not do this to pressure them, but to encourage Corinth to complete its own help.

For today: Christian generosity springs from a grateful and free heart, not from obligation. Ask yourself what you can give with joy, whether money, time, or help, even if your situation is limited.
exp.6:13:
Paul says that he had spoken well of the Corinthians before Titus, and that he was not put to shame. The word "boasting" in the verse means that he felt proud of them and spoke with confidence about them. The phrase "is found a truth" means that what he said turned out to be true, just like everything else he had told them.

Paul writes to a church with which he had experienced tension. Titus had visited Corinth and came back encouraged by how they received him. Paul rejoices because his confidence in them was not in vain. Scholars debate exactly which offense the context refers to, but the general tone is one of relief and closeness.

Today, we can speak well of others and trust the best in them. We can also live in such a way that those who believed in us do not have to be ashamed. A kind word and sincere confidence encourage many.
exp.8:14:
It says we give thanks to God for a gift so great that it cannot be described in words. "Gift" is a gift, and "unspeakable" means it cannot be fully expressed or explained. The Bible does not clarify here what that gift is, and so some think it is Christ himself, others the grace of God in general, and others the unity among believers.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth as he encourages them to give an offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. In the verses before, he explains that this generosity leads others to praise God. With this phrase he closes the topic, reminding them that all human generosity springs from what God has already given first.

For today: before you give your time, your money, or your help, stop to thank God for what you have received. A grateful life becomes generous with more joy.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that the ministry of condemnation, that is, the law of Moses that exposed sin and declared people guilty, came with glory. But the ministry of righteousness, the gospel that declares us righteous before God, has a much greater glory.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some teachers were questioning his authority. He compares the ministry of Moses, with the law engraved on stone and the shining face, with the ministry of the new covenant. He does not despise the law, which was also glorious, but he affirms that the grace of Christ surpasses it.

For today: do not spend your life trying to earn God's acceptance through your own effort. Receive each day the forgiveness and righteousness that Christ has already given you, and let that gratitude move you to obey him with joy.
exp.2:0:
Paul asks the Corinthians two questions. He asks whether he is beginning again to commend himself, and whether he needs, as some others do, letters of recommendation to you or from you. The word "commend" here means to praise or recommend oneself, and "letters of recommendation" are letters that introduce and vouch for a person.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, the church he himself helped to bring into being. He had earlier been accused of boasting, and there were teachers who arrived carrying letters of endorsement. Paul does not need that: the changed lives of the Corinthians are his best proof. Commentators see here a touch of gentle irony.

For today: we do not need to boast about our service or seek applause. What speaks most about us is the fruit that God produces in our own life and in the lives of others. Live in such a way that your testimony is your best letter.
exp.11:7:
Paul says that he prayed to the Lord three times that the thorn would be taken away from him, the suffering that troubled him. The verse's comment on the word "asked" is removed here, since it refers to wording not in the verse your reader sees; the phrase "that it might depart from me" means that it would leave his life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry against those who boasted of their achievements. He speaks of his revelations and of a thorn in his flesh that kept him humble. It is not known for certain what it was: some think of an illness, others of opposition or persecution. The text does not make it clear. Christ did not remove it, but answered him: "My grace is sufficient for thee."

Today we can pray sincerely and persistently about what hurts us. If God does not take it away, that does not mean he has abandoned us. His grace sustains us, and his power can be shown in our weakness.
exp.7:20:
Paul says that he and his companions work to do what is good and right, not only because God sees them, but also because people watch them. "Honest things" here means good, honorable, and clean things. The phrase "providing for" means taking careful pains to look after something.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth about the offering that was being gathered to help the poor believers in Jerusalem. The churches had chosen a brother to travel with Paul and take care of the money. That way, no one could suspect him or accuse him of mishandling it.

If you handle money or responsibilities in the church or at work, do it with clarity and order. Keep records, report honestly, and let others help review. In this way you guard your witness and honor God.
exp.9:14:
Paul says that he does not boast beyond what belongs to him, nor claim credit for work that others have done. He hopes that the faith of the Corinthians will keep growing, and that through this his own service among them will be greatly extended, always within the field that God assigned to him. "Measure" here means the measure or area of work that God gave him. "Be enlarged" means that his work should reach further.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some teachers praised themselves and took pride in the work of others. Paul answers that he did arrive in Corinth with the gospel, and that he does not take over the effort of others. His desire is to keep moving forward and to preach in places where Christ is not yet known.

For today: honestly recognize what God has entrusted to you, and do not dress yourself up with the work of others. Rejoice when others grow in faith, and remember that all credit belongs to the Lord.
exp.10:28:
Here Paul says that he identifies himself with others in their suffering. The English reader sees "weak" and "offended," so the old-word glosses are rewritten for those words in the verse. To be weak means to lack strength, whether in body or in faith. To be offended means to stumble or fall into sin. To burn speaks of an inward fire: pain, anguish, and zeal for that person.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry against teachers who considered themselves superior. Instead of boasting of successes, he lists his sufferings. After speaking of beatings, weariness, and dangers, he mentions his heaviest burden: the care of all the churches. His pastoral love made him feel others' struggles as his own.

For today: love those who suffer or stumble truly. Do not judge them from a distance; draw near, listen, pray for them, and walk alongside them with tenderness and patience.
exp.3:16:
This verse compares two things: our present sufferings and the glory that is coming. Paul says that the affliction is "light" and passing, lasting only a moment, while the glory is a weight that is far greater and eternal. The word "worketh" means it produces or prepares us for that glory. The phrase "far more exceeding" means extraordinary, beyond all measure.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom he had served in the midst of persecutions, weariness, and dangers. He does not deny that he suffers; in other passages of the letter he describes his pains in detail. But he looks at his suffering in the light of eternity and of the inner renewal that God gives him each day. Some understand that suffering "produces" the glory; others understand that it prepares for it under God's grace.

Today, when you are going through a difficulty, do not minimize it, but do not let it be the only thing you see. Ask God to renew your spirit today, and remember that your pain is not the last word.
exp.10:1:
Paul says he feels a holy jealousy for the Corinthians, a care that comes from God himself. He uses the image of a wedding: he has promised them in marriage to one husband, Christ. His hope is to present them in the end as a pure bride, that is, faithful and without stain in their love for him. Here "jealousy" means an intense and protective concern, not envy.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he himself founded. Other teachers have arrived who present a different Jesus and a different gospel, and Paul feels obligated to defend his ministry. That is why he asks them to bear with him even though it may seem foolish for him to speak about himself this way. He is worried that they will be led astray.

For today: examine whether your faith remains centered on the simple Christ of the gospel. Compare what you hear with what the Bible says, and guard your loyalty to Jesus above passing trends or attention-grabbing teachings.
exp.9:13:
Paul says that he is not going beyond the limits God gave him. He does not boast beyond what is right, as though his work had never reached Corinth. The phrase "stretch not ourselves beyond our measure" means boasting or acting outside the field that was assigned. He affirms that he did reach them, because he was the one who brought them the gospel of Christ.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who had been influenced by other teachers who praised themselves and questioned his authority. He answers with firmness but without arrogance: his authority does not come from comparing himself with others, but from the work God entrusted to him. Corinth was part of that work.

For today: serve where God has placed you, without comparing yourself with others or boasting of what you did not do. Be thankful for your place, do well what was entrusted to you, and let God be the one who gives you worth.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that God, who comforts those who are cast down, encouraged Paul and his companions when Titus arrived. The word "cast down" here refers to those who are discouraged or downcast. The word "nevertheless" means "but," and "comforted" means "encouraged and gave relief."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He was in Macedonia, weary, with conflicts on the outside and fears on the inside. He was waiting for news of how the Corinthians had received his previous letter, which had been harsh. Titus arrived with good news that they had repented and held him in high regard. Paul sees in this the hand of God.

God often comforts us through people. If you are downcast, do not isolate yourself: accept the company of other believers. And you can be the one who brings encouragement to someone through a visit, a phone call, or a sincere word.
exp.12:5:
Paul says that he hopes the Corinthians will come to recognize that he and his team have not failed the test.

Paul writes to a church that doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. Just before, he told them to examine themselves to see whether they were in the faith. If Christ lives in them, that very fact confirms that Paul's ministry was genuine. He does not defend himself out of pride, but for their good.

For today: before judging others, examine your own faith honestly. Ask yourself whether Christ is really guiding your life, and be humble enough to receive correction.
exp.7:23:
Paul asks the Corinthians to show visibly, before the churches, that their love is real. The word "shew" means "show," and "proof" refers to clear evidence. He also reminds them that he has been proud of them ("our boasting on your behalf"), and he wants that confidence not to remain only in words.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the offering for the poor believers in Judea. He is sending Titus and other brothers to help them complete that collection. He had spoken well of the Corinthians before other churches, and now he encourages them to respond with deeds.

For today: Christian love is seen in concrete actions. Think of a nearby need, whether of a brother or sister or of your church, and help generously and sincerely, not to appear good, but to joyfully do what you say you believe.
exp.10:0:
Paul asks the Corinthians to put up with him for a little while as he speaks like a "fool." By "foolishness" he means boasting about himself, which he himself considers foolish. The words "bear with" are the same as "put up with," and "but" is the same as "yet." So the sense is: "I wish you could put up with this foolishness of mine; indeed, do put up with me."

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, a church he himself founded. Some outstanding "super-apostles" were influencing them and questioning Paul's authority. To defend himself, he feels forced to speak of his achievements and sufferings, even though it makes him uncomfortable. He does it out of love and concern for them, as the following verses explain.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we let ourselves be carried away by impressive voices rather than by the simplicity of the gospel. Compare what you hear with what Christ teaches in the Bible, and listen humbly to those who truly care for you.
exp.9:12:
Paul says he will not boast beyond what is rightly his. He rejoices only in what God assigned to him, and that includes having reached the Corinthians.

Paul is answering some people in Corinth who criticized him, saying he was bold in his letters but weak when he was present in person. Others were praising themselves and comparing themselves with one another. Paul does not join that game. He affirms that God gave him a field of work, and that Corinth fell within that field because he preached the gospel to them first.

Today we can learn not to compare ourselves with others or boast about what others do. Ask yourself what God has entrusted to you: your family, your work, your church. Serve it with humility, and be thankful for what He does through you.
exp.12:8:
He says that Paul is glad when he is weak, and the Corinthians are strong in the faith. Here "perfection" speaks of maturity and being restored, not of having no flaws. Paul desires that the church grow and be complete in its Christian life.

The apostle Paul writes to a church with conflicts, where some questioned his authority. Before visiting them, he invites them to examine themselves and to correct what is wrong. He does not seek to look good or to show his power. If they obey the truth, he will not have to use his authority with firmness, and he does not mind appearing weak or "reprobate."

Today we might ask ourselves whether we are glad to see others grow, even when we receive no recognition. A good leader, parent, teacher, or friend serves so that others become stronger, without needing to feel superior.
exp.10:3:
Paul says that if someone comes preaching a "different Jesus" from the one he already proclaimed to them, or if they receive a different spirit or a different gospel from the one they accepted, they put up with it very easily. "Bear with" means to endure or tolerate. It is a rebuke: the Corinthians accept readily what they should not.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, which he himself founded. He feels a holy jealousy for them, like a father protecting his daughter before her wedding. He fears they will be deceived, as Eve was, and drift away from the simplicity that is in Christ. Some teachers presented themselves as superior to him, and that is why he mentions "those very eminent apostles." Interpreters debate exactly who they were.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what Jesus says in the Bible. If it presents a different Christ or a message that changes the gospel, do not accept it just because it sounds attractive.
exp.10:16:
Paul says that what he is about to say now, that is, his boasting or "glorying," he does not speak as if the Lord were commanding it as an example to follow, but "as it were foolishly." It means: as a fool would say it. The "confidence of boasting" refers to the assurance with which he sets himself to talk about himself.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whom he founded in the faith. Some "super apostles" had won them over with their credentials and showy claims, and they were discrediting Paul. He dislikes boasting, but he feels compelled to do it, as in a game of fools, to show that his accusers are not superior. Scholars debate how much of this is irony, but the tone is clear: he does it with reluctance.

For today: boasting about our achievements is not the way of the Lord. If we ever must defend our name or service, let us do it with humility, brevity, and without losing sight of the fact that all true glory belongs to Christ.
exp.2:14:
Paul says that even in his time, when the law of Moses was read aloud in the synagogues, something covered the hearts of the listeners. The "veil" is a picture: it means they could not grasp the true meaning of what they heard. The reading aloud refers to the public reading of Scripture.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and recalls that Moses covered his face after speaking with God (Exodus 34). He compares the old covenant with the new. Many Jews listened to the Scriptures, but did not see Christ in them. Interpreters explain the veil in different ways, but all agree that the lack of understanding is taken away when a person turns to the Lord.

We can read the Bible with humility and ask God to open our understanding. Reading alone is not enough; we need to look for Christ in its pages, and He gives us light and freedom.
exp.7:4:
It says that the Christians of Macedonia gave far more than Paul and his companions had hoped for. First they gave their own selves to the Lord, and then they put themselves at the disposal of the apostles, according to the will of God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish a collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He holds up as an example the churches of Macedonia, who gave generously even in the midst of poverty. Paul explains that their generosity came from having first given themselves to the Lord.

For today: before asking how much to give, ask yourself whether your heart is truly surrendered to God. When He has first place in your life, giving with joy, time, money, or service becomes a natural response and not a burden.
exp.8:5:
What it says: Paul uses the image of sowing. Whoever sows little will reap little; whoever sows generously will reap generously. "Sparingly" means with little, with stinginess. "Reap" means to harvest. "In blessings" speaks of giving generously, as a blessing to others.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the offering they had promised for the needy believers in Jerusalem. He sends some brothers ahead so that everything is ready and the help does not seem to be given grudgingly. Interpreters debate whether the harvest refers to material rewards, spiritual ones, or both. The text that follows emphasizes the grace of God, not a simple exchange.

For today: When you have the chance to help, prepare your help in advance and give with joy, trusting that God cares for the one who gives generously.
exp.6:12:
Paul says that he and his companions were encouraged when they saw how the Corinthians responded. But what gave them the greatest joy was seeing Titus happy. Here "refreshed" means renewed and reassured, and "comfort" means encouragement or consolation. Titus was refreshed by the way all of you treated him.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth after a strained relationship. He had sent them a firm letter to correct a problem, and they reacted with sincere sorrow and a desire to make things right. Titus carried that letter and returned with good news. Paul shares his relief and acknowledges that Titus's encouragement was also a blessing.

For today: when someone corrects you with love, respond with humility and a desire to change. Also, encourage those who serve others, since their work is often hard, and a good welcome can renew their spirit.
exp.11:5:
Paul says that if he wanted to boast about his spiritual experiences, he would not be a fool, because he would be speaking the truth. But he prefers not to do so. "Fool" means someone who lacks sense, and "glory" here means to boast or brag about oneself. His desire is that no one should think more highly of him than what they see of his life or hear from his own lips.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were impressed by teachers who boasted of visions and power. He had spoken of an extraordinary experience that happened about fourteen years earlier, and now he stops. He prefers to be judged by his conduct and his words, not by experiences that no one can verify. Right after this, he speaks of his weakness.

For today: you do not need to impress others with your achievements or spiritual experiences. Let your life and your words be what speak about you, with humility and honesty.
exp.10:6:
Paul asks a question with a touch of irony: Was it a sin for me to humble myself so that you could be lifted up, because I preached the gospel of God to you without charge? "Lifted up" means raised up, or enriched spiritually. "Without charge" means without taking any payment.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his authority against certain "super apostles" who were criticizing him. He did not charge them, working with his own hands and receiving help from other churches. Some in Corinth seem to have seen this as a sign of weakness. Paul shows them that his sacrifice came from love and not from a lack of worth.

For today: let us not measure the value of a service by its shine or its price, but by the love with which it is done. And when someone serves with humility, let us thank them instead of looking down on them.
exp.6:7:
Paul says that the letter he wrote to them caused them sorrow. He had felt regret for sending it, but now he no longer regrets it, because he sees that the sorrow lasted only a short time and brought something good.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. He had sent them a firm letter to correct them, and he feared he had hurt them too much. Titus has just arrived with good news: the Corinthians had been grieved and wanted to do what is right again. Many think that letter is different from 1 Corinthians, although there is no full agreement.

A correction given with love may hurt, but sometimes it is the path to healing. If someone corrects you sincerely, do not harden yourself right away; ask God for humility to listen. And if you must correct someone else, do it with kindness, truth, and a desire to help.
exp.7:22:
It says that if anyone asks about Titus, he is Paul's companion and a fellow worker for the good of the Corinthians. And if people ask about the other brothers, they are sent by the churches and bring honor to Christ. The word "fellowhelper" means a helper or fellow worker. The phrase "concerning you" means "about you."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth while he arranges a collection to help believers in need. He explains who will carry that money, so that no one has reason to doubt them. He wants everything to be done openly, as he said in the previous verse: in the sight of the Lord and in the sight of people.

For today: if we handle money or responsibilities in the church, it is wise to do so with order, clarity, and trustworthy people. Honesty does not diminish faith; rather, it protects the good name of Christ.
exp.8:3:
Paul says that if some Christians from Macedonia come with him to Corinth and find that the Corinthians do not have the offering ready, there would be shame. Paul would be ashamed, and even more so the Corinthians, for having spoken with such confidence about them. Paul's point is that the boasting he made about them would prove empty if the gift were not prepared.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He had praised them before the Macedonians for their good will. Now he sends some brothers ahead so that everything will be ready and the offering will be given generously and willingly.

For today: if we have promised to help someone, let us keep our word on time and from the heart. We can set aside what we offered, without leaving it until the last moment, so that our generosity is sincere and not a rushed obligation.
exp.2:1:
Paul tells the Corinthians that they are the letter that recommends him and his companions. That letter is not written on paper but inscribed on Paul's heart. The word "epistle" means a letter, and "known and read of all men" means that everyone can recognize it and read it.

Paul writes to a church that he himself founded in Corinth. Some were carrying letters of recommendation to gain acceptance, and others were questioning Paul's authority. He answers that he does not need that kind of paper: the changed lives of the Corinthian believers are the proof that his ministry is genuine.

For today: our lives are what people read most about Christ. You might ask yourself: what does the way I treat others say about Jesus? Ask the Spirit to help you live in such a way that others see his work in you.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the more we suffer for following Christ, the more comfort we receive from Him. The "sufferings of Christ" are the hardships that come from belonging to Him and serving Him; some believe they also refer to sharing in his sufferings. To "abound" means to be present in great amounts, overflowing and growing. "Consolation" is encouragement, relief, and strength.

The apostle Paul is writing to the church in Corinth. He has just praised God as the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. Paul had gone through great trials in his ministry, and he explains that both his suffering and his comfort also serve to encourage the Corinthians.

Today, when you go through a trial because of your faith or because you are doing what is right, do not think that God has left you alone. Ask Him for His comfort with confidence, and then use what you received to encourage another person who is suffering.
exp.7:10:
Paul asks the Corinthians to finish what they started. "Carry out the doing of it" means to complete the work. They had a good desire and were ready and eager. Now they should show that same readiness in following through, giving according to what they have, that is, according to their means.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Corinthians had begun the collection the year before, but it seems it had stalled. Paul encourages them by reminding them of the example of Christ, who, though rich, became poor for their sake.

For today: if God has placed in your heart the desire to help someone or to serve in some way, do not let it remain a good intention. Take a concrete step this week with what you really have, without comparing yourself to anyone.
exp.12:4:
This verse says that the Corinthians should examine themselves to see whether they are truly in the faith. "Examine" and "prove" mean to evaluate honestly. "Reprobate" means failing the test, like a counterfeit coin. Paul reminds them that Jesus Christ is in them, unless they fail the test.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, with whom he had tensions. Some doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. Paul turns the question back on them: instead of examining him, let them examine themselves. Their changed lives would be evidence of his ministry.

For today: before judging others, take a moment alone with God and ask yourself honestly how your faith, your love, and your obedience are doing. Ask him to show you what you need to correct.
exp.10:13:
We should not be surprised that there are false teachers who appear good, because Satan himself disguises himself as an "angel of light," that is, as something good and bright. "Transforms himself" means that he changes his appearance, pretending to be what he is not.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, to whom he had preached the gospel. Others had arrived who presented themselves as superior apostles and criticized him. Paul says they are "deceitful workers" who disguise themselves as apostles of Christ. His warning seeks to protect the church from deception.

For today: it is not enough that someone sounds pious, is pleasant, or speaks about God. Compare what they teach with the Bible, see whether they exalt Jesus, and look at the fruit of their lives. Ask God for discernment.
exp.3:15:
They say that Paul and his companions do not give up or lose heart. "Not losing heart" means not becoming discouraged or surrendering. The "outward man" is our physical life, the body, which is wasting away, that is, it grows weaker through suffering and the passing of time. The "inward man" is the life of the spirit, which is being renewed day by day: God strengthens it each day.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth and speaks of the hardships he endures while preaching the gospel. He has just said that God, who raised Jesus, will also raise them. For this reason he sees his trials as something temporary, compared with the eternal glory he mentions next.

For today: when tiredness, illness, or problems wear you down, do not lose heart. Set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible, so that God renews your inner strength and reminds you of the hope that cannot be seen.
exp.4:5:
What it says: Paul affirms that believers live with courage and confidence, even knowing that while we are in this earthly body, we are away from the direct presence of the Lord. The verse's word for "traveling" means walking like travelers in a foreign land, on the way to our true home. Being "confident" means having good courage without losing heart.

Context: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, speaking of hardships and of the fragile body, which he calls a temporary tent. His courage comes from the fact that God has already given them the Spirit as a guarantee of what is to come. The following verses explain that we walk by faith and not by sight.

For today: When you feel tiredness, pain, or doubt, remember that this life is not the end. Take a few minutes today to thank God for his promise, and ask him that his Spirit give you confidence to keep going with hope.
exp.3:7:
It says that Paul and his companions go through many trials, but they are not defeated. The words "troubled" and "distressed" in the verse mean that they feel pressure and hardship, and "perplexed" means being without resources or not knowing what to do. "Despair" means losing all hope. So they suffer, but there is always a way out and a hope.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth and speaking about his ministry. He has just said that they carry the treasure of the gospel in fragile vessels, that is, in fragile people. This shows that the strength comes from God and not from them. These opposing phrases express that idea: they are weak, but God sustains them.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, you do not have to pretend that it does not hurt. Be honest with God about your weariness and your doubts, and trust that his power sustains you even when your own strength runs out. Also ask for the support of your Christian community.
exp.11:0:
Paul says that boasting is neither helpful nor fitting for him. Even so, he is going to speak of "visions" and "revelations," that is, experiences in which the Lord showed him things in a supernatural way. To "glory" means to boast or to take pride in oneself. Here, "doubtless" means "it is true that."

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who doubted his authority because some "super-apostles" bragged about their achievements. To defend himself, Paul feels compelled to speak about himself, but he does so reluctantly. In the verses that follow he speaks of a man in Christ, and many understand this to refer to himself, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: if God is at work in your life, give thanks and speak of Him with humility. Do not use your spiritual experiences to feel superior, but to encourage others.
exp.7:11:
The verse says that when someone has first a sincere desire to give, it is accepted according to what that person has, and not according to what they do not have. A willing mind is a heart that is ready and eager, and "accepted" means pleasing or well received.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, who had begun to gather an offering to help the poor believers in Jerusalem. About a year had passed, and Paul encourages them to finish what they started. He makes clear that he is not asking for more than is possible, but that they should give according to their means.

For today: do not compare yourself or become discouraged by how little you can give. Give with joy what you have, whether time, help, or money, and keep the promise you have made.
exp.12:6:
He says that Paul and his companions pray to God that the Corinthians do nothing wrong. But they do not pray this so that they themselves look good, or so that others see their ministry as approved. They pray it so that the believers do what is good, even if that makes Paul appear rejected or worthless. The word "reprobate" here means rejected or without value. Your verse reads "do" and "ye," which mean "do" and "you."

Paul writes to a church that doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ spoke through him. Before visiting them, he asks them to examine themselves. He would rather they put things right, so that he does not have to correct them harshly, even if that leaves him without proof of his authority.

For today: seek the good of others without thinking about your own image. If you help, correct, or advise someone, ask yourself whether you are doing it so that they grow in Christ or so that you look good. Pray for that person with that heart.
exp.10:4:
Paul says that he is confident he was in no way less than those "very chiefest apostles." The word "whit" means "at all" or "in the least," so his point is that he counted himself equal to them. He does not speak with empty pride, but defends his calling.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who are worried that teachers will come preaching "another Jesus" and another gospel. Some of them boasted of their authority and eloquence, and looked down on Paul. He calls them "very chiefest apostles" with a certain irony; scholars debate whether he means the leaders in Jerusalem or those deceptive teachers. Many think he means the latter, though this is not entirely certain.

Today, let us not measure a teacher by his fame or his fine speaking, but by whether he faithfully preaches Jesus and the gospel we receive in the Bible.
exp.11:17:
Paul says that he asked Titus to go to Corinth, and that he sent another brother with him. Then he asks questions: Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act with the same spirit and walk in the same steps? The phrase "walk in the same steps" refers to the way one lives and conducts oneself, the manner of walking through life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against suspicions. Some were saying that he had manipulated them, perhaps through his messengers, to get money from them. His answer is to remind them that Titus and he acted with the same honesty. Interpreters agree that the subject is integrity in handling financial help, although the text gives no further details.

For today: live with transparency, so that our actions and those of the people who work with us can withstand any question. And when someone doubts us, respond with humility, honesty, and clear facts.
exp.11:6:
It says that Paul received revelations so extraordinary that he was at risk of becoming full of pride. To prevent this, God allowed "a thorn in the flesh," that is, something that caused him constant pain, like a thorn stuck in the body. He calls it "the messenger of Satan" sent to "buffet" him, that is, to strike him. "Lest I should be exalted above measure" means beyond what is fitting, or excessively.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against teachers who boasted of their achievements. Earlier he spoke of an incredible spiritual experience, but he prefers to speak of his weaknesses. We do not know for certain what the thorn was: some think of an illness, others of opposition or persecution. The Bible does not make it clear.

For today: God can use our limitations to keep us humble and dependent on Him. When something hurts and does not go away, remember that His grace is enough for you.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that all of God's promises find their "Yes" in Jesus Christ. In other words, they are fulfilled and confirmed in him. That is why we also say "Amen" through him, and this brings glory to God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians because some were accusing him of changing his plans and of not being reliable. He answers that his message is not uncertain, wavering between yes and no, because God is faithful and Christ is God's firm answer. Then he says that God himself confirms us and gives us his Spirit as a guarantee.

For today: when you doubt that God will do what he has said, look to Jesus. Trust his promises and respond with a sincere "Amen," thanking him and living with hope.
exp.7:14:
Paul quotes Scripture to say that when God provides, no one is left without what they need. Whoever gathered much did not have anything left over, and whoever gathered little did not come up short.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to encourage them to help the poor believers in Jerusalem with an offering. He is asking for fairness: not that they would go without, but that they help now, so that at another time they themselves might be helped. The quotation comes from Exodus 16:18, when God gave the manna in the wilderness.

Today, if God has given you more than you need, ask yourself whom you can help with it. Sharing generously trusts that God cares for everyone.
exp.2:7:
Paul asks a question that already carries its own answer: if the ministry of the law, carved in stone, came with glory, how much more glorious will the ministry of the Spirit be! "Ministry" means service or work done in service to God. "Spirit" here refers to the Holy Spirit, who works in the new covenant.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his service against those who questioned it. He compares the covenant given through Moses, whose glory was temporary, with the new covenant, where the Spirit gives life. Some understand the "letter" as the written law without God's power to change the heart; this is how the text presents it.
