For today: do not rely only on your own efforts to keep rules. Ask the Holy Spirit to transform you from within, and serve others trusting in his power, not your own.
exp.3:0:
It says that Paul and his companions have a ministry, which here is called "administration" (the KJV uses "ministry"), that is, a charge to serve. They received it through God's mercy, not through their own merit. That is why "we faint not" means that they do not give up or lose heart.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with whom he has had tensions. Some questioned his authority and his way of preaching. Just before this, he spoke of the new covenant and the glory of the gospel. Now he explains why he remains firm despite the difficulties: his ministry springs from the grace of God.

For today: when you grow tired of serving or of doing good, remember that God gave you that calling with mercy. You do not depend on your own strength, but on his grace. Ask him for encouragement today and take the next step with humility.
exp.8:10:
God enriches us in every way, so that we can be generous on every occasion. That generosity, when it reaches others, leads them to give thanks to God. The phrase "thanksgiving" in the verse is the word that matters here, and it appears in the verse as "thanksgiving to God."

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to encourage them to finish their offering for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He reminds them that God provides the seed and the bread, and that the offering not only helps those in need but also leads many to praise God.

For today: if God has given you something, whether money, time, or abilities, ask yourself whom you can bless with it. Give with joy and simplicity, trusting that God takes care of you, and let your generosity lead others to thank Him.
exp.5:8:
They are seen by people in one way, but the reality is another. They seem "unknown," yet God knows them well. They seem "dying," yet they are still alive. To be "chastened" refers to being corrected or struck with suffering, but not destroyed.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth to defend his ministry. Some were criticizing him and doubting him. He shows them that, although he goes through trials, dishonor and dangers, his service is genuine. This list of contrasts is part of that defense, and many scholars see it as an example of how God sustains his servants in the midst of suffering.

For today: if you feel unnoticed, exhausted or undervalued for serving God, remember that He sees you and sustains you. Your worth does not depend on the opinion of people, but on the fact that God knows you.
exp.10:17:
It says that, since many boast of human things ("after the flesh": achievements, background, prestige), Paul will also boast. To "glory" means to brag or take pride. "Foolish" here means senseless or without good judgment.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, whom he founded in the faith. Some teachers who presented themselves as superior were influencing them and attacking Paul. He dislikes boasting and warns that he is not speaking in the Lord's way, but with irony, like a fool. He does this so that they will see the emptiness of that pride, and shortly afterward he will boast of his weaknesses and sufferings.

For today: do not be impressed by someone who boasts of titles, success, or appearance. Measure people by their character and faithfulness to Christ. And examine your own heart: what do you boast in?
exp.0:0:
Paul introduces himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ, that is, one sent by Him, and he clarifies that he holds this role by the will of God, not by his own decision. Together with Timothy, whom he calls "the brother," he writes to the church of Corinth and to all the saints of Achaia. "Saints" are the believers set apart for God. "Unto" is an older way of saying "to," and "you" is the same word for all readers.

Paul writes this letter to a church that he himself helped to found, but with which he had experienced tensions and criticism about his authority. For that reason he begins by reminding them where his calling comes from. Achaia was the region of Greece where Corinth was located. Including all the believers in the area shows that the message was meant for a wider community.

For today: God calls us to serve without placing ourselves at the center. We can act with humility, remembering that our place in his work is a gift, and walk alongside other brothers and sisters.
exp.4:0:
Paul says that we know something with certainty: if our body, which is like a house or tent where we live on earth, is destroyed, God has prepared another house for us. The word "house" in the verse refers to the place where one lives, and the word "tabernacle" points to a temporary dwelling like a tent. That house was not made by human hands, and it is eternal, in the heavens.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth, and he is speaking about the sufferings and fragility of life. In the previous chapter he speaks of our outer self that is wasting away. He wants to encourage them not to lose hope. Interpreters debate whether that house is a raised body or a heavenly dwelling; the text does not fully clarify this.

For today: when tiredness, sickness, or loss weigh on you, remember that this life is not all there is. Rest in God's promise and live with hope and confidence.
exp.0:11:
Paul says that what fills him with a healthy pride is having a clear conscience. He affirms that he has lived with simplicity (plainness, without hidden motives) and with godly sincerity (honesty that comes from God). He did not rely on worldly wisdom, that is, on human cleverness or tricks for persuading people, but on the grace of God. This is how he behaved in the world, and even more so toward the Corinthians.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, with which he had a strained relationship. Some were questioning his motives and his conduct. Just before this, he spoke of his sufferings and of how God had delivered him. Here he defends himself with humility, appealing to his conscience and to what the Corinthians had already seen in him.

Today, strive to live so that your conscience is clear before God: be transparent in your words and decisions, and do not depend on appearances or cunning, but on his grace.
exp.8:1:
Paul says that he knows the eagerness of the Corinthians. He is proud of them and has told the Macedonians about it: that Achaia (the region of Corinth) had been ready since last year. Moreover, their enthusiasm stirred many others to take part.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth about the collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. The Corinthians had promised to help, but they had not yet finished. Paul praises them warmly and at the same time, gently, encourages them to complete what they began, so that their good witness does not remain only in words.

For today: a good intention needs follow-through. If God has placed in your heart the desire to help someone or to serve in some way, do not leave it pending. Set one concrete step this week and carry it out with joy. Your example can encourage others.
exp.0:21:
It says that God himself has marked us with a seal and gave us the Holy Spirit as a pledge. A pledge is a down payment or guarantee: a first installment that assures the rest will come. The seal shows that we belong to God and that he protects us. All of this takes place in our hearts, that is, in the innermost part of the person.

Paul speaks here, writing to the Christians in Corinth. He had been criticized for changing his travel plans, and people accused him of not being firm in his word. He answers that God is faithful and that it is God who sustains all of us in Christ. That is why his word is not careless.

For today: when you doubt your faith or your future, remember that your security does not depend on your own strength, but on the fact that God has sealed you and given you his Spirit. Rest in that and live with confidence and gratitude.
exp.1:10:
He says that Paul does not want Satan to take advantage of them and deceive them. He affirms that the believers know Satan's schemes, that is, his plans and tricks for bringing people down. The phrase "lest Satan should get an advantage of us" means that Satan would gain an advantage over us.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a painful situation, in which someone had been disciplined. Now he asks them to forgive that person and restore him. He says that he too forgives, in the presence of Christ. Paul sees that refusing to forgive could lead to division and excessive sorrow, and that this would open a door to the enemy.

For today: if someone wronged you and has repented, do not hold a grudge. Forgiveness is not weakness; it is a way of protecting unity and of leaving no room for the enemy's deceptions.
exp.2:2:
Paul says that the Corinthians are like a letter from Christ, written by the Spirit of the living God and not with ink. This letter is not carved in stone but written on human hearts. The phrase about "fleshy tables" means hearts that are sensitive and ready to respond. The word "ministered" means that Paul and his companions served as the ones who delivered it.

Paul is writing to the believers in Corinth. Some were questioning his authority and asking for letters of recommendation. Paul answers that the best proof of his ministry is the changed lives of the people themselves. The "tables of stone" bring to mind the law of Moses, and he contrasts that with the inward work of the Spirit.

For today: people can read our lives more than our words. Ask the Spirit to soften your heart, and let the way you treat others show who Christ is.
exp.4:12:
Plain-language translation of the verse of 2 Corinthians 5:13:

This verse says that Paul and his companions act for God and for the Corinthians. The words "be beside ourselves" and "be sober" in the verse above convey the same idea: being beside yourself means being out of your mind or not in your right senses, and being sober means being of sound mind, with a clear head. If they seem excessive in their devotion, it is for God; if they are sensible and balanced, it is for the good of others.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, among whom some were criticizing him and boasting about outward appearances. We do not know for certain what "be beside ourselves" refers to. Some think he was speaking of intense spiritual experiences; others, that he was being accused of being a fanatic. What is clear is that, according to the next verse, the love of Christ was what moved him.

For today: serve God with sincere devotion, even when others do not understand, and treat people with clarity, patience and good sense. Ask yourself what the other person needs, not how it affects you.
exp.11:16:
Paul asks: "Did I take advantage of you through any of the men I sent to you?" It is a question that expects the answer "no." The word "take advantage" here means to exploit them by deceit, especially where money is concerned.

Paul is speaking to the Corinthians and defending himself. Some were accusing him of being crafty and of having manipulated them, perhaps by charging them through the co-workers he sent. Paul had decided not to be a financial burden to them. So he appeals to what they themselves saw: Titus and the brother who went with him acted with the same spirit and the same steps as he did, that is, with integrity.

For today: live with transparency, especially in how you handle money and in your service. If someone doubts your intentions, respond with clear actions and with humility, always seeking to build others up and not defending yourself out of pride.
exp.0:1:
Paul wishes the believers in Corinth grace and peace. Grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is the calm and reconciliation that He gives. Both come from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul writes together with Timothy to the church in Corinth and to the believers throughout all of Achaia. It was a common greeting in his letters. Here it matters, because his relationship with the Corinthians had been strained, and he writes to them with affection and sincerity before speaking about comfort in the midst of suffering.

For today: before speaking with someone you have difficulties with, ask God for grace and peace for that person and for yourself. Beginning with a kind attitude can open the door to a healthy conversation.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was announced to the Corinthians by Paul, Silas and Timothy, and that in him there is no double meaning: he is not "Yes" and "No" at the same time. On the contrary, in Christ everything is "Yes," that is, firmness and faithfulness. Here "preached" simply means proclaimed. The name "Silvanus" is another name for Silas.

Paul is speaking to the church in Corinth. He had changed his travel plans, and some accused him of being fickle and of saying whatever suited him. He answers that his message does not change, because Christ does not change. He defends his integrity by relying on the faithfulness of God.

For today: work to make your word trustworthy. Keep what you promise and, if you have to change a plan, explain it honestly. And when you doubt God, remember that in Jesus you always find a firm "Yes."
exp.3:13:
This verse says that Paul is certain of something: God, who raised up Jesus, will also raise us up through Jesus. And he will present us, both him and the Corinthians, before Him together. "Being certain" means "having full confidence." "Raised up" means "brought back to life."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth in the middle of suffering and persecution. He explains that his work brings exhaustion and danger of death, but that others receive life through that message. He quotes Psalm 116: believing and speaking go together. His hope in the resurrection gives him courage to keep preaching, and that is why he does not give up.

For today: when you are tired, sick, or discouraged, remember that your hope does not depend on what you see now. If God raised up Jesus, he will also keep his promise to you. That confidence helps you keep serving, speaking about your faith, and encouraging others.
exp.12:3:
He says that Christ was crucified in weakness, meaning he allowed himself to be taken to the cross without defending himself with human power, but now he lives by the power of God. Paul says that he too is weak, as Christ was, but that he will live with Christ by that same power, for the good of the Corinthians.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some doubted his authority and asked for proof that Christ was speaking through him. The Corinthians saw his weakness and took it as a sign of failure. Paul answers that Christ's weakness on the cross did not prevent the power of God from acting. He also warns that, if he comes again, he will act with firmness.

For today: do not be afraid to recognize your limits. Your weakness is no obstacle to God. Place it in his hands and trust that he can work with his power in your life and through you.
exp.10:10:
Paul asks the Corinthians: "Why didn't I ask you for financial support? Could it be that I don't love you?" And he answers right away: "God knows that I do love you." He puts God forward as the witness of his heart.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, which was being influenced by false apostles. Paul had preached among them without charging them, and some may have read that as a lack of affection or of authority. He explains that he will keep doing this in order to deny those deceptive teachers the chance to boast that they are equal to him. His motives were love and purity of intention, not coldness.

For today: love does not always show itself the way others expect. When someone misreads your good intentions, don't defend yourself with anger. Place them before God, keep serving with integrity, and let time reveal your heart.
exp.9:0:
Paul says that he himself pleads with the Corinthians, appealing to the gentleness and kindness of Christ. The word "but" stands at the start of his sentence, and "I beg you" is "I plead with you." He describes his manner as gentle, and some say that when he is present in person he is humble, timid or weak, but that from afar, by letter, he is bold.

Paul writes to a church that he founded, but in which some were criticizing him and doubting his authority. They accused him of being strong only in his letters. He does not answer with pride, but by recalling the character of Christ. The verses that follow show that he prefers to correct with tenderness, although he is willing to be firm if necessary.

When someone criticizes or questions us, we can respond with the gentleness of Christ instead of defending ourselves harshly. Being kind does not mean being weak; it means being able to use firmness with humility and love.
exp.10:21:
Paul asks three questions and to each one he answers "so am I." Hebrews, Israelites, and the seed of Abraham are three ways of saying that he belongs to the people of God, with their language, their history, and their inheritance. "Seed" means descendants.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were being influenced by some teachers who boasted of their Jewish background and their credentials to gain authority. Paul says he is speaking as a fool because he does not enjoy boasting, but he does it so that they will not be deceived. Later he will show that his true credential is his sufferings for Christ.

For today: do not be impressed only by titles, appearance, or polished presentation in someone who teaches. Examine their character, their faithfulness to Christ, and their humility. And when you have to defend yourself, do it with simplicity, without seeking your own glory.
exp.8:7:
This verse says that God has the power to make all grace abound toward you, that is, his favor and his blessings. Thus, always having all sufficiency in all things, you will be able to abound in every good work. The phrase "that you" introduces the purpose of God's grace, and "all sufficiency" refers to having enough of everything you need.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth to encourage them to take part in the collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He reminds them that God loves the one who gives with joy, and that God is the one who provides what is needed so that they can give generously.

For today: when you have the opportunity to help someone, do not think only about what you lack. Trust that God can supply what you need, and give with joy, knowing that your generosity is a good work that he himself supports.
exp.2:12:
Paul says that he does not act like Moses, who covered his face with a veil. According to the text, Moses did this so that the Israelites would not keep their eyes fixed on the end of what was going to be set aside, that is, what was going to be brought to an end and no longer hold force. The glory on Moses' face was temporary.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends his ministry. He compares the old covenant, given through Moses, with the new covenant in Christ, which is more glorious and lasting. For this reason he preaches openly, hiding nothing. Interpreters explain the exact purpose of the veil in different ways, but Paul uses it as an image of a truth that was not yet seen clearly.

Today we can draw near to God with sincerity, without pretending or hiding what we are. Let us ask Him to help us see Christ clearly throughout the Scriptures and to speak of Him with confidence and humility.
exp.10:29:
It says that, if it becomes necessary to boast about something, Paul will boast about his weaknesses. The word "necessary" is what the verse calls "needs," and "boast" means to take pride in something. "Weakness" refers to whatever makes a person feel fragile or limited.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, who were impressed by teachers who boasted of their credentials and achievements. To answer them, Paul makes a list of his sufferings and of his care for the churches. Instead of showing power, he shows what serving cost him. Then he tells how he had to escape from Damascus, a story that is anything but glorious.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong in order to serve God. You can be honest about your limits and trust that God works in the middle of them. Today, share a real difficulty with someone and thank God for sustaining you.
exp.11:20:
Paul fears that, when he returns to Corinth, God will humble him in front of them, and that he will have to grieve over many who sinned earlier and did not repent of the impurity, sexual immorality, and shameless, unrestrained behavior they committed. Impurity is uncleanness, sexual immorality is sexual relations outside of marriage, and shameless behavior is conduct without modesty, unrestrained. "Had sinned" means that they had already sinned.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, a church he founded. He is about to make his third visit to them, and he speaks to them frankly, not to defend himself, but to build them up. The sin that does not lead to repentance grieves him more than his own shame. His sorrow is that of a spiritual father who loves his people.

For today: do not minimize sin or hide it. If there is something God is showing you, repent soon. And if you see a fallen brother or sister, approach them with tears and love, not with contempt.
exp.8:9:
God is the one who gives seed to the sower and also bread for food. He himself will multiply what you sow and make the fruits of your righteousness grow, that is, of your good and generous deeds. The seed that is sown, or the field that is sown, and the increase, or the harvest, are the things the verse speaks of.

Paul writes to the believers in Corinth to encourage them to finish the offering they were gathering for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He uses the image of the field: God provides what is necessary, and generosity produces a harvest that leads many to give thanks to God. Paul does not promise personal wealth, but that God will give enough for them to keep doing good.

Today we can give with confidence, knowing that what we have comes from God. Think of a specific need near you and share some of your time, money, or resources with joy.
exp.9:5:
He says that Paul and his companions are ready to correct every act of disobedience, but first they wait until the obedience of the Corinthians is complete. Being ready means being prepared. "To punish" here is understood as correcting or disciplining with authority.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some questioned his authority and saw him as weak. He explains that their struggle is spiritual, not fleshly. Before acting with firmness, he gives the church time to respond well. Interpreters debate exactly what correction he had in mind, but his patience and his desire to build up, not to destroy, are evident.

For today: when someone needs correcting, let us do it with patience and with a desire to restore. And let us first examine our own obedience to Christ before demanding it of others.
exp.5:2:
It says that Paul and his companions take care not to give anyone a reason to stumble. The word "offence" here means something that causes others to stumble or turns them away from the faith. The word "blamed" means criticized, discredited, or spoken ill of. So the purpose is that the work of proclaiming the gospel not be discredited by their conduct.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, with whom he had a difficult relationship. He has just pleaded with them not to receive the grace of God in vain, for now is the time of salvation. As a messenger of Christ, he knows that his way of living can either help or hinder the message. For this reason, in the verses that follow, he describes how he has remained faithful even in suffering.

For today: before you speak or act, ask yourself whether your conduct helps others see Christ or pushes them away. Guard your honesty, your treatment of others, and your words, not seeking applause but honoring God.
exp.7:8:
The verse says that the Corinthians already know the grace of Jesus Christ: though he was rich, for their sake he became poor, so that through his poverty they might become rich. Grace is a favor that no one has earned. The word "ye" in the verse means "you," the people Paul is writing to.

Many understand the riches of Christ as his glory with the Father, and his poverty as his humble coming. The riches we receive are spiritual: forgiveness and life with God.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to finish a gift they had started to help other believers who were in need. He does not give them a command, but uses the example of Christ to encourage their sincere generosity.

For today: before you give or help someone, remember how much you have received from Christ. Look for a concrete way to give with joy, according to what you are able to do, without pressure or pride.
exp.11:11:
Paul reminds the Corinthians that the signs that prove a true apostle were seen among them. These signs came along with great patience, that is, with steady endurance in the middle of hardships. There were also "signs, wonders, and mighty deeds," which are powerful works of God that go beyond the ordinary.

Paul writes in his second letter to the Corinthians. Some false teachers looked down on him and boasted that they were superior. That is why Paul, reluctantly, has to defend his authority, even though he feels foolish doing so. Notice that he mentions patience first, and only afterward the miracles. For him, suffering endured is part of the proof.

For today: let us not measure a leader only by how impressive or striking he is. Let us also look at his character, his humility, and his endurance. And when we are called to serve, let us seek to be faithful and patient, trusting that God works through our weakness.
exp.5:3:
He says that Paul and his companions seek to show themselves in every way as true servants of God. They demonstrate this by enduring with great steadiness (persistence, not giving up) the hardships, the lacks, and the situations with no way out. The word that describes how they conduct themselves can be rendered as behaving or carrying themselves as God's servants.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth, with whom there was tension and doubt about his ministry. In the previous verse he asks not to give any cause for stumbling, so that the gospel would not be criticized. For this reason he presents his conduct and his sufferings as proof of his sincerity. A long list of trials and virtues follows.

For today: our witness is seen most in how we respond when things become difficult. We can ask God for patience in a specific difficulty, and take care that our conduct does not hinder others from coming closer to Christ.
exp.5:0:
Paul says that he and his companions work together with God ("workers together with him"). From that position they ask the Corinthians for something important: that they not receive the grace of God without effect. Receiving it "without effect" means without fruit, without changing their lives. The words "beseech you" mean "we earnestly encourage you."

Paul writes to a church that had already believed, but that had problems and doubts about his ministry. In the previous chapter he spoke of reconciliation with God through Christ. Now he pleads that this reconciliation be seen in actions. Some understand the "him" to be God; the context suggests this.

Today we can ask ourselves: is my faith only something I believe, or does it also change how I treat others? Today, for example, you can ask someone for forgiveness or help someone who needs it, as a grateful response to the grace you have received.
exp.10:31:
Here Paul tells how, in Damascus, the governor who served under King Aretas placed guards over the city in order to seize him. The guards watched the gates, and the aim was to capture him.

Paul is speaking to the Christians of Corinth, who were being swayed by critics who boasted of their achievements. Instead of boasting of power, Paul recounts with irony a humiliating scene: he had to escape in secret. He says he will boast of the things that show his weakness. Historians debate how Aretas came to have control in Damascus, and there is no certain explanation for it.

For today: you do not need to appear strong to be useful to God. Your moments of weakness, fear, or shame can show that strength comes from Him. Be honest about your limits and trust in His care.
exp.10:32:
He says that Paul escaped from Damascus when people were looking to arrest him. They lowered him through a window that opened onto the city wall, inside a basket, which was a large wicker or rope basket. In this way he escaped from the hands of those who wanted to seize him.

Paul is speaking to the Corinthians. Some were criticizing him and boasting of their own glories, so he answers by listing his sufferings as an apostle. He mentions this escape almost at the end of the list, and it is an unheroic scene: he does not flee with strength, but hidden and lowered down by others. Scholars understand that with this he shows that his boast lies in his weakness, where God's help is seen. This episode also appears in Acts 9:23-25.

For today: do not be ashamed of the moments when all you can do is escape, ask for help, or depend on others. God can care for you in your weakness too, and sometimes he uses ordinary people as his basket of rescue.
exp.3:4:
Paul says that he and his companions do not announce themselves. Their message is that Jesus Christ is the Lord. And they, instead of seeking honor, present themselves as servants of the believers, for Jesus' sake. The verse as your reader sees it reads "your servants," so the comment about the old spelling and the word meaning "of you" is removed.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some questioned his authority and admired more showy teachers. Just before this, he speaks of how many do not see the light of the gospel because they are blinded. So he clarifies that his message does not revolve around his own prestige, but around Christ, and that his service is humble, not for showing off.

For today: before speaking about your faith or serving in the church, ask yourself whether you are seeking to be admired or seeking for Jesus to be known. Serve with humility and always point toward Christ.
exp.2:4:
It says that we are not capable on our own, not even of thinking something good as if it came from ourselves alone. The word "sufficient" in the verse means able, having what is needed to carry out a task. Paul affirms that all his ability comes from God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, where some were questioning his authority. He answers that his ministry does not rest on letters of recommendation or on his own talents. The proof is the believers themselves, changed by the Spirit. That is why his confidence is in God, who made him a minister of a new covenant.

Today we can serve with humility and without fear. If God is the one who equips us, we need neither to boast nor to feel useless. Before a difficult task, pray: "Lord, I cannot do it alone, but you can."
exp.9:9:
This verse repeats what some people were saying about Paul: that his letters were "weighty and powerful," meaning serious and forceful, but that in person he seemed weak, and his way of speaking was "contemptible," that is, of little worth or deserving scorn.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some critics questioned his authority. He insists that the power God gave him is meant to build up, not to tear down. In the verses that follow, he makes clear that he is the same whether writing from a distance or present in person. Some scholars think his critics judged by appearance and eloquence.

For today: let us not measure people by their presence or by the way they speak. And if someone criticizes us, we can respond with consistency, being the same in what we say and in what we do.
exp.6:9:
This verse says there are two kinds of sorrow. The sorrow that is in line with God's will is the pain we feel when we see that we have failed Him. That sorrow moves us to change direction, and it brings salvation and leaves nothing to regret. The sorrow of the world, by contrast, is the sorrow that produces death.

Paul writes to the Corinthians after having sent them a harsh letter to correct them. At first he doubted that he had hurt them, but now he rejoices, because their sorrow led them to change. Many believe the letter refers to a problem of discipline in the church, though it is not known with certainty what it was.

For today: when you feel bad about a mistake, ask yourself whether your sorrow draws you closer to God and moves you to correct yourself, or whether it only sinks you into guilt or wounded pride. Bring your failure to God and take a concrete step of change.
exp.5:4:
It says that Paul and his companions endured concrete hardships: "stripes" are blows with a whip or rod; "imprisonments" are times of being locked up; "tumults" are crowds or disturbances, sometimes violent; "labours" are hard work and exhaustion; "watchings" are nights without sleep; "fastings" are times without eating, whether from necessity or by choice.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry. He wants them to see that he is not a self-interested preacher, but a servant of God. For that reason he presents what he suffered as proof of his sincerity. Some of these hardships appear in other passages, such as 2 Corinthians 11:23-27. It is not certain which fastings were voluntary and which were forced.

Today, this invites us not to measure service to God only by comfort or success. If we face difficulties for doing good, we can continue with patience, trusting that God sustains those who serve him sincerely.
exp.10:9:
Paul states with great seriousness: "As the truth of Christ is in me," that is, he speaks as someone who belongs to Christ and does not lie. He says that this boasting, or reason for pride, will not be stopped by anyone, that no one will take it away or silence him throughout the regions of Achaia, where Corinth was. That boast is having preached the gospel without charging the Corinthians anything.

Paul is writing to a church where some teachers presented themselves as superior to him. He had preached to them free of charge, and the brothers from Macedonia supplied his needs. Now he defends his conduct and affirms that he will continue the same way, so as not to give a pretext to those who criticized him.

For today: serve with generosity and without hidden self-interest. Take care that the way you serve does not hinder the gospel or give reason to doubt your sincerity.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that the Lord is the Spirit, and that where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. "There" means in that place or in that life. The liberty here is the one God gives, not the freedom to do whatever one wants.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth. He compares the reading of the law of Moses, which many Jews heard with a veil over the heart, that is, without understanding Christ, with the new life in the Lord. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. Some interpret the phrase "the Lord is the Spirit" to mean that Christ and the Spirit act together, without Paul saying that they are the same person.

Today, if you feel bound by guilt, fear, or empty religion, come to God with sincerity. Ask him that his Spirit give you understanding and liberty to live in his truth and love.
exp.4:6:
We believers say that we live and make decisions by trusting God and his promises, and not only by what we can see with our eyes. Our way of living day to day is guided by faith, and sight refers to what can be seen or confirmed right now.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth. He tells them that while we live in this body, we do not yet see the Lord face to face, and so we are away from him. Even so, God gave us his Spirit as a guarantee of what is to come. For this reason Paul is encouraged and confident, even in the face of death.

When you face a difficult situation and see no way out, you can take the next step trusting that God is faithful. Pray, seek his guidance in the Bible, and act with integrity, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that the same God who commanded light to shine out of darkness at creation is the one who has shone in our hearts. That light gives us the knowledge of God's glory, which can be seen clearly in the face of Jesus Christ. The word "face" here means the countenance or presence of Jesus, and "shine" means that something becomes clear and understood.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his ministry. Earlier he said that the god of this age (many understand this to refer to Satan) blinds unbelievers. Paul makes clear that he does not preach himself, but Christ. Later he will say that he carries this treasure in clay jars, that is, in fragile people.

For today: if understanding God is God's own work, we can pray with humility, asking him for light, and look to Jesus to know him better. We can also share what we know of Christ without boasting, remembering that the light comes from God.
exp.7:16:
Paul says that Titus did accept Paul's request to visit the Corinthians, but he was also so eager to help them that he chose to go on his own initiative. "Exhortation" means an appeal or encouragement; "eager" means very attentive and ready; "of his own accord" means he went by his own decision.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth to encourage them to finish the offering they had promised for the poor Christians in Judea. He had earlier said that God placed the same care for them in Titus's heart. In this way he shows them that Titus comes with a good attitude, and that the collection will be handled responsibly.

Today we can learn that serving God is not just doing what we are asked. We can ask Him to give us a willing heart, to help others with joy and on our own initiative, not out of obligation.
exp.9:17:
It says that speaking well of oneself is not enough to be accepted. What truly counts is the approval of God. "Praise" here means to commend or to boast, and "approved" means that someone has passed the test and is recognized as genuine.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, where some teachers were commending themselves and criticizing Paul. He answers that he does not compare himself with others or claim credit for other people's work. His service was to bring the gospel to new places, and if anyone wants to boast, let them boast in the Lord.

For today: before seeking applause or trying to impress others, ask yourself whether what you do pleases God. Serve with sincerity, recognize that every good fruit comes from Him, and let God be the one who gives the final recognition.
exp.9:8:
Paul says that he does not want it to seem as if he is trying to terrify the Corinthians with his letters. In today's language: "I do not want them to think I only write to frighten them." The word "terrify" in the verse means to frighten or put fear into someone.

In this letter Paul defends his authority as an apostle. Some in Corinth criticized him, saying his letters were strong but that in person he was weak and unimpressive. He clarifies that the authority God gave him is for building up the church, not for tearing it down. His goal is to help them grow, not to dominate them.

For today: when we correct someone, let us do it to build up and restore, not to terrify or impose ourselves. May our words and our lives agree, and may love guide every piece of advice.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that he and his companions felt in themselves that they already had a sentence of death. This happened so that they would stop trusting in their own strength and place all their trust in God, who raises the dead. The word "sentence" here means a verdict or judgment.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth. He tells them about a very hard trouble he went through in Asia, so heavy that they doubted they would come out alive. We do not know with certainty exactly what it was; scholars offer different ideas. What matters to him is that God delivered them, and that the Corinthians can help by praying.

For today: when you feel without strength or without a way out, do not see it as the end. It may be an invitation to let go of control and rest in God. Bring your situation to him in prayer, and ask others to pray with you as well.
exp.5:11:
Paul tells the Corinthians that he is not holding back his affection from them. The Greek-derived idea behind "straitened" is that they are cramped, with little room. "Bowels" refers to the innermost part of a person, where feelings are born. In other words: "We have made plenty of room for you in our hearts, but you have shrunk back in your affection toward us."

Paul is writing to a church that had grown cold toward him, partly because of criticism and doubts about his ministry. He has just spoken of his sufferings and his open heart. Now, like a father, he asks them to respond with the same openness. Some think this prepares his call to separate from harmful influences, but that is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if there is someone who has served you with love, such as a pastor or a relative, check whether your heart has closed because of pride or misunderstandings. Take the first step and make room for them again.
exp.7:17:
Paul says that together with Titus he sent another brother, one who is highly praised in all the churches for his service in the gospel. The word "together" in the verse means "at the same time, in company," so the sense is that this brother went along with Titus. "Praise in the gospel" refers to a good testimony about his work in spreading the good news.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to encourage them to finish the gift they had promised for the poor believers in Jerusalem. That is why he sends Titus with two trusted companions. The Bible does not give this brother's name, and various ideas have been suggested since early times, but there is no certainty.

Today we can learn that the handling of money in the church should be done with openness and by people of good reputation. If we serve in something that involves other people's resources, it is wise to work as a team and give a clear account, so that no one has reason for suspicion.
exp.11:19:
Paul says he is worried about what he will find when he visits the Corinthians. He fears they will not be as he wants them to be, and that he will not be as they would want him to be, meaning he may have to correct them firmly. He lists problems: contentions (fights), envyings (jealousy), wraths (anger), strifes (divisions), backbitings (speaking badly of others), whisperings (gossip), swellings (pride and arrogance), and tumults (groups opposing one another).

Paul writes this letter as an apostle and the founder of the church in Corinth. He has just defended his own conduct and that of Titus, and he insists that he does everything to build them up. His desire is not to shame them, but for them to repent before he arrives. His tone shows the affection of a spiritual father, but also seriousness.

For today: examine your relationships in the church, your family, or your workplace. If there is gossip, pride, or resentment, do not wait for someone to confront you. Ask God for forgiveness, and seek peace with that person this week.
exp.10:7:
Paul says that he "robbed" other churches, meaning that he acted like someone who takes what does not belong to him. By this he means that those churches supported him with their gifts while he was serving the Corinthians. The word "serve" in the verse means to minister to them, and "for nothing" means free of charge.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth where some people criticized him and favored other teachers who charged fees. He uses strong, almost ironic language to defend the fact that he preached to them without cost. Scholars understand his words as deliberate exaggeration, not as an actual theft.

Today we can support generously those who serve in the church and in missions. And those who serve can do so with humility, without seeking their own benefit, thinking of the good of others.
exp.8:8:
This verse quotes Scripture to show what a generous person is like. "He hath dispersed abroad" means he has distributed freely and widely, like someone scattering seed. "He hath given to the poor" means he has given to those in need. And "his righteousness remaineth for ever" means that his good work, his upright life before God, is not lost.

The quotation comes from Psalm 112:9.

Paul writes to the Christians in Corinth and encourages them to take part in the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He reminds them that God loves the person who gives cheerfully and that He Himself supplies what is needed so they can give. Here he uses the Psalm as an example of what God approves.

For today: decide in your heart on one concrete way to help someone in need, without pressure or sadness, trusting that God takes care of you while you take care of others.
exp.12:13:
The verse text did not appear in your message, but from the context it is Paul's closing blessing: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen." Here "communion" means fellowship, a shared partnership. Paul wishes that believers would live out the undeserved kindness of Christ, the love of the Father, and the unity that the Spirit gives.

Paul closes his second letter to the Corinthians, a church marked by many tensions and much pain. He writes to them with affection, but also with firmness, and ends with a blessing that names the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. Many see here one of the clearest expressions of the Trinity in the New Testament, although the word itself does not appear.

For today: when you say goodbye to someone, try to bless them sincerely, asking God to give them grace, love, and fellowship, and not just a "take care."
exp.2:5:
God himself, it says, made Paul and his companions able to serve in a new covenant. The word translated "able" here means capable or fit. This covenant is not based on the written code taken only as external rules, but on the Spirit. The letter kills because it shows sin and brings condemnation but gives no power to change; the Spirit gives life.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, where some questioned his authority. He does not boast in his own strength, but says that his ability comes from God. He then compares the ministry of Moses, carved on stones, with the ministry of the Spirit, which is more glorious. Some interpreters debate the details of what "letter" and "spirit" mean, but the general contrast is clear.

Today, do not live your faith only as a list of duties. Ask the Holy Spirit to transform your heart, and trust that God equips you for what he entrusts to you.
exp.0:22:
Paul says that God is his witness, and he says it with great seriousness, calling on his own soul as a pledge. He affirms that he had not yet returned to Corinth out of consideration for them. To be "lenient" here means he wanted to be patient with them and spare them, avoiding a painful visit. Calling God as witness is like saying: "God knows that I am telling the truth."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth. He had changed his travel plans, and some were accusing him of being unreliable or of not taking them seriously. He explains that it was not out of carelessness. He preferred to wait so as not to arrive with harsh rebukes, and so give them time to correct themselves. The verses that follow make clear that he does not seek to dominate their faith, but to help their joy.

For today: when you have to correct someone, ask yourself whether you are doing it with love and patience. Sometimes waiting and speaking calmly serves better than reacting immediately. And if you are misunderstood, explain your motives with humility and sincerity.
exp.10:30:
Paul says that God himself, the Father of Jesus, who is to be praised forever, knows that what he is saying is true. It is like calling God as a witness. "Blessed forever" means worthy of being praised eternally. "I do not lie" means that he does not exaggerate or make anything up.

Paul writes to the Corinthians and defends himself against some teachers who boasted of their achievements. He, however, chooses to speak of his weaknesses and sufferings. Since what he is saying is hard to believe, he solemnly affirms that he is telling the truth, and right away he recounts his escape from Damascus in a basket.

For today: let us speak with honesty, without embellishing the story to impress. Living as someone who knows that God sees everything helps us to be sincere, even when we admit our weaknesses.
exp.10:25:
Paul lists the dangers he faced on his journeys: rivers to cross, robbers, attacks from his own people (the Jews) and from the Gentiles (those who were not Jews). He also spoke of dangers in the city, in the wilderness, at sea, and among "false brethren," that is, people who claimed to be believers but were not.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to defend his calling as an apostle. Some proud teachers considered themselves superior to him. Instead of boasting of successes, Paul points to his sufferings for serving Christ. It is a way of saying: my life given over to God proves that my service is genuine.

Today, this reminds us that serving God can cost us and is not always comfortable. If you go through hardships for doing what is right, do not think that God has abandoned you. Keep going with humility and confidence in Him.
exp.8:12:
It says that the help the Corinthians send is a real proof of their faith. Those who receive it glorify God for two reasons: because they see that the Corinthians obey the gospel of Christ, and because the Corinthians are generous toward them and toward all people. The words "ministration," "professed," and "distribution" in the verse point to this: the help given is service, the confession is their declaration that they believe, and the sharing is giving from their goods.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth and encourages them to finish a collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem. He explains that this offering not only meets needs but also produces thanksgiving to God. For Paul, true faith shows itself in concrete deeds. It also unites believers from different places.

For today: help generously someone in your church or community who is in need. Do it simply, so that your faith is seen in action and others give thanks to God.
exp.0:7:
Paul says he does not want the brothers and sisters to be unaware of the trouble he went through in Asia. It was a burden far beyond the ordinary, so heavy that it went past his strength. It was so severe that he doubted whether he would come out of it alive.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with whom his relationship is at times strained. He has just spoken of the comfort God gives in suffering. Now he honestly shares his own ordeal. We do not know with certainty what it was; scholars have proposed different ideas, and the text does not make it clear. What is clear is that Paul reached his limit, and that God delivered him.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong. Paul admitted his weakness before others. If you are overwhelmed, tell God and a trusted person. That is where comfort can begin.
exp.11:10:
Paul says he has acted like a fool by boasting about himself, but that the Corinthians forced him to do it. The verb "compelled" means they pressed him into it, and "very chiefest apostles" refers to those supposed superior apostles. He claims that he was not in any way less than them, though he admits that in himself he is "nothing."

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, where some arrogant teachers criticized him and questioned his authority. The Corinthians should have defended him, but they did not. That is why he boasts reluctantly, with a certain irony. Scholars debate who these "very chiefest apostles" were: the apostles in Jerusalem, or the false teachers who passed themselves off as them.

For today: when you have to defend your calling or your work, do it with humility and without pride. Remember that whatever is valuable in you comes from the grace of God, not from your own merits.
exp.7:7:
Paul says he is not giving a command. He wants to confirm that the love of the Corinthians is genuine, and he does this by comparing it with the eagerness of other churches. "Love" is the meaning of the word here, and "eagerness" refers to the earnest effort others have shown. To "test" something means to check that it is genuine.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth about the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Earlier he told them how the churches of Macedonia gave generously, even though they were poor. Paul does not force them, but he invites them to finish what they had already begun. When he speaks of testing, he is not accusing them; he is encouraging them to show by their deeds what they say they feel.

For today: love shows itself in concrete actions. Think of a promise of help you left unfinished and carry it out gladly, without anyone having to force you.
exp.1:14:
For we are a sweet savour of Christ to God, and this fragrance reaches everyone: those who are being saved and those who are perishing. The phrase "those who are perishing" refers to people who reject the message of the gospel.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a difficult time, and he tells them that he was anxious because he could not find Titus. Even so, he thanks God because his ministry moves forward like a victory procession. Some understand the image of the fragrance as the incense of those Roman processions, though this is interpreted in several ways. What is clear is that Paul speaks of his service and of how the message is received in different ways.

For today: live and speak with sincerity, without boasting or manipulating others. Not everyone will respond well, and that does not mean you have failed. Your task is to be faithful to Christ, and God takes care of the outcome.
exp.9:10:
Paul says that the one who criticizes him should consider this: what he is in his letters when he is far away, that same he will be in his actions when he is present. "Such an one" is the person who is judging him. "Word" refers to what he says, and "deeds" to what he does.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, and some were accusing him of being bold only in writing, but weak and unimpressive in person. He answers that there is no difference between his written message and his actual conduct. He wants to correct them with authority given by God, but he prefers that it not be necessary to do so harshly.

For today: let us seek to make our words and our lives agree. May we be the same people in public and in private, in messages and in person. Integrity gives weight to what we say.
exp.1:13:
Paul gives thanks to God because He always leads us in triumph in Christ. Moreover, through us He makes the knowledge of God spread everywhere like a pleasing fragrance.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians after a period of strain with them. He had just described his distress in Troas, where he did not find Titus, who was bringing news from Corinth. Even so, he suddenly praises God. The image seems to be drawn from a victory procession, although some scholars understand it in other ways. The central point is that the triumph belongs to Christ, not to Paul.

We can trust that God works even in moments of worry or apparent failure. Our task is not to draw attention to ourselves, but to live and speak of Christ with sincerity and kindness, so that others may perceive something of his goodness in us.
exp.12:0:
Paul says this is the third time he is getting ready to visit the Corinthians. Then he quotes an old rule: every matter is confirmed by the word of two or three witnesses. "Matter" here means an issue or a case, and "shall be established" means it will be made firm or settled.

Paul is writing to a church with which he has had conflicts. Some doubted his authority, and others were still living in sin. He uses the rule from Deuteronomy 19:15 to warn that, if he comes and there are accusations, he will deal with them justly. Scholars debate whether the "witnesses" are his visits or his warnings, or whether the phrase refers to the people who would give testimony. Even so, the general meaning is clear: he wants a fair process.

For today: before accusing or judging someone, seek out the facts and listen calmly. Do not repeat rumors. If there is a conflict, work to resolve it with truth, humility, and order.
exp.5:12:
Paul asks the Corinthians to respond to his affection in the same way. He says he speaks to them as his own children and urges them: "be ye also enlarged," that is, open your hearts and make more room for affection, without shutting yourselves off or keeping your distance.

Paul is writing to a church with which he has had tensions. He reminds them that he has spoken to them frankly and that his heart is open toward them. According to him, the coldness does not come from his side, but from theirs. After this appeal, he goes on to warn them about partnerships with unbelievers, and some understand that the two themes are related: opening the heart to fellow believers and separating from what harms the faith.

For today: if there is a brother or sister in the faith from whom you have drifted apart through pride or hurt, take a concrete step, such as a phone call or an honest conversation, to open your heart to them again.
exp.6:14:
He says that Titus feels a very deep affection for the Corinthians. "Inward affection" was an old way of speaking about the deepest feelings of the heart, so the word "inward" here points to that. That affection grows when Titus remembers that all of them received him with respect and a willing spirit. The phrase "with fear and trembling" does not speak of being afraid of a person, but of seriousness and humility in receiving someone sent with an important message.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth after a tense relationship with them. He had sent Titus, and Titus returned encouraged by how they responded. Paul is glad because what he had said about them turned out to be true. Some understand the obedience as obedience to Paul and his letter; the text does not detail this further.

For today: when someone corrects you or serves you with good intentions, receive them with humility. And when you see good responses in others, express your affection and gratitude to them.
exp.0:3:
He tells us that God comforts us in all our tribulation, and that this comfort does not stop with us. We receive it so that we can encourage others who are going through any kind of distress, using the same comfort that God gave us.

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, with Timothy at his side. Before speaking of his own sufferings, he praises God as the Father of mercies. Then he explains that his afflictions and his comfort also serve to strengthen the Corinthians.

For today: if God sustained you in a difficult moment, do not keep that story to yourself. Think of someone who is suffering something similar, draw near, listen to them, and humbly tell them how God comforted you.
exp.6:3:
Paul says that he has great confidence in the Corinthians and that he takes pride in them. He is filled with comfort, and his joy overflows, despite all his afflictions.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Corinth, with whom he had had tensions. He asks them to welcome him again with openness, assuring them that he never harmed or deceived them. Shortly before, he had sent them a firm letter, and now Titus brought him good news about how they received it. That is why his spirit changes, even though he had been very distressed.

For today: even in difficult times, we can find comfort in seeing that God works in other people. Today, encourage someone with specific words of appreciation.
exp.1:8:
Paul says that one of the reasons he wrote his earlier letter was to "have experience" of them, that is, to test them to see whether they were obedient "in all things." The word "experience" here means to check or come to know something through a test.

Paul is speaking to the believers in Corinth. It is thought that he is referring to a case of church discipline, perhaps that of a man who had done something serious. Now that this person was sorry and deeply saddened, Paul asks them to forgive and comfort him. Scholars do not fully agree on who this person was or which letter this was, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: obedience to God includes both correcting with truth and forgiving with love. If someone has repented, ask yourself whom you need to comfort and restore, instead of keeping them at a distance.
exp.10:27:
Paul says that, besides all the hardships he has already listed, there is something that presses on him every day: the care of all the churches. The phrase "cometh upon me daily" suggests burdens that pile up and arrive all at once, and "care" means sincere concern, attention, and worry for others.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians and is forced to defend his ministry, because some teachers were questioning it. Instead of boasting of his achievements, he lists his dangers and weariness. Here he shows that his greatest burden was not physical but his love, as a shepherd, for the communities he had helped to be born in the faith.

For today: if you look after others, whether in the family, the church, or at work, it is normal to feel that weight. Do not carry it alone. Bring it to God in prayer, and look for fellow believers with whom you can share the task.
exp.4:17:
It says that all the new things Paul has just described come from God. He reconciled us to himself through Christ, that is, he brought us near to himself and ended the hostility. He also gave us a task: to announce that reconciliation.

Paul is writing to the Corinthians, a church under strain, where some questioned his authority. He has just spoken of the new creation, and here he explains that this change is not a human achievement. He also maintains that his ministry comes from God, not from himself.

For today: if God brought you near to himself without your having earned it, you can live with gratitude instead of fear. And you can share that good news with humility, inviting others to be reconciled to God, just as you were welcomed.
exp.4:7:
Paul and his companions say they have courage and confidence. Even so, they would prefer to leave this earthly body and be in the presence of the Lord. The word "but" in the verse is the English equivalent of the connecting word that begins the verse, and "to be absent from the body" refers to leaving this life through death, while "to be present with the Lord" means being beside Him.

Paul writes to the Christians of Corinth in the midst of suffering and weakness. Earlier he spoke of the body as a fragile tent. Here he explains that death does not frighten him, because faith leads him to expect Christ. He then makes clear that, whether at home or away, he wants to please the Lord.

For today: when you are afraid or worn out, remember that your hope does not end with this life. That hope is not an excuse to live without energy, but a reason to live today in a way that pleases Christ, with faith and confidence.

sum.10: Paul defends his ministry to the Corinthians because he is afraid that false apostles, who disguise themselves as servants of Christ, will lead them away from the simplicity of the gospel. With irony, he compares himself to these men and lists his sufferings: beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, and his worry for the churches. He would rather boast about his weakness, such as when he escaped from Damascus in a basket.
sum.5: Paul urges the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain, because now is the time of salvation. He describes how he and his companions serve God with patience, truth, and love, even in the midst of suffering. Then he asks the Corinthians to open their hearts and turn away from whatever defiles, since they are the temple of the living God.
sum.9: Paul defends his authority against those who say he is bold in his letters but weak in person. He explains that the weapons he uses are not human but are powerful through God, and that he will be just as firm in person as he is by letter. He clarifies that he does not compare himself with others or boast about himself, since whoever boasts should boast in the Lord.
sum.2: Paul says that the believers in Corinth are a "letter from Christ," written by the Spirit on the heart, and that his ability as a minister comes from God. He contrasts the old covenant, which was of the letter, with the new covenant of the Spirit, which gives life and freedom. Those who look at the glory of the Lord are being transformed more and more into his likeness.
sum.11: Paul tells of a man who, fourteen years earlier, was caught up to paradise, but he says he would rather boast about his weaknesses. God did not take away his "thorn in the flesh," and told him, "My grace is sufficient for you," because his power is made perfect in weakness. Paul defends his authority and his love for the Corinthians, and he fears that he may find sin among them.
sum.12: Paul warns that he will come to Corinth for the third time and that he will not spare those who continue to sin. He asks them to examine themselves to see whether they are truly in the faith, because Christ lives in them. He writes to build them up, not to tear them down, and he closes by encouraging them to live in peace and unity, with a blessing.
sum.1: Paul explains that he wrote with tears, out of love, so that he would not have to come to the Corinthians in sorrow. He asks them to forgive and comfort the person who caused the pain, so that Satan does not take advantage of them. He describes his anxiety in Troas at not finding Titus. He gives thanks to God, who always leads him in triumph in Christ, and he speaks with sincerity.
sum.3: Paul says that, because of God's mercy, he does not lose heart when preaching Christ with truth, even though some do not see it because they are blinded. He explains that he carries the treasure of the gospel in "jars of clay," weak but held up by God's power. Although his body is wasting away, his inner self is being renewed, and he looks to what is eternal and cannot be seen.
sum.0: Paul and Timothy greet the church in Corinth and praise God, who comforts us in our troubles so that we can comfort others. Paul tells how, in Asia, he came close to death and learned to trust only in God, who raises the dead. He explains that he changed his travel plans in order to look after the Corinthians, and that God's promises are "Yes" in Christ.
sum.4: Paul says that even though our earthly body will wear out, God is preparing an eternal home for us in heaven. That is why we live by faith and seek to please him, knowing that we will all give an account before Christ. The love of Christ, who died for everyone, makes us new creations. God has reconciled us to himself and asks us to invite others: "Be reconciled to God."
sum.8: Paul encourages the Corinthians to have the gift they promised ready for the Christians in need, and he sends brothers to help them get it prepared. He teaches that God loves the person who gives with joy and willingness, and that God provides so that they may abound in every good work. Their generosity will supply the needs of others and will lead many to give thanks to God.
sum.6: Paul encourages the Corinthians to cleanse themselves from everything that defiles and to live in holiness, and he tells them that they hold a place in his heart. He shares that God comforted him with the arrival of Titus, who brought good news. He teaches that godly sorrow leads to a repentance that brings salvation, while the sorrow of the world brings death.
sum.7: Paul encourages the Corinthians to finish their collection for the needy believers, holding up the churches of Macedonia as an example. Though those churches were poor, they gave joyfully. He reminds them that Christ became poor to make us rich, and he asks them to give according to what they have, so that there is fairness. He sends Titus and other brothers to manage the gift with integrity.
